# Real-instrument toolchain: sampler (samples) + pluck (physically modelled plucked strings)

For writing **original scores** for Lemo-Opuscar style films. Everything is synthesised offline with numpy/soxr at **48 kHz**, with the same conventions as `sfx.py` (`SR`, `add()`, `limit()`).
The goal is "sounds like a real instrument": use samples wherever possible (97 instruments, real recordings), and fill in the folk plucked strings the sample libraries lack (guqin, pipa, shamisen…) with physical modelling (11 presets).

- Preview: the repo has no ready-made preview files (`core/audio/*.wav` is not in git, and not in the sample packs either). After downloading a sample pack, use the pattern in section 1 to play a small root-fifth-octave motif on each instrument and render a stretch to listen to yourself
- Sample libraries: `core/audio/instruments/` (lossless FLAC; each library keeps its original LICENSE/README). Not in git; download per library, only the ones the film uses: `sh tools/fetch.sh instruments <lib>` (`vsco2ce` 395 MB, `vcsl` 271 MB, `salamander` 218 MB, `freepats` 397 MB, `karoryfer` 74 MB), or `instruments all` (about 1.4 GB). The Source column in section 5 is the library an instrument lives in: VSCO 2 CE → `vsco2ce`, VCSL → `vcsl`, Salamander → `salamander`, FreePats and MuldjordKit → `freepats`, Karoryfer → `karoryfer`
- Index: `core/audio/instruments/index.json` (every library's pack ships a copy: pitch, velocity layer, onset point and level of every sample; ready to use on import, no rebuild needed)

---

## 1. Thirty-second start

```python
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, '.')   # run from the repo root
import numpy as np, soundfile as sf
from core.audio import sampler as S, pluck as P
from core.audio.sfx import SR, add, limit

x = S.note('cellos', 'D3', 4.0, vel=.6)            # cello section long note, 4 s (extended seamlessly if the sample is too short)
y = S.hit('snare', 'roll', .5)                       # unpitched hit: instrument + variant + velocity
z = P.pluck('guqin', 'A3', 3, vel=.7, bend=[(.5, 0), (.9, 2)])   # guqin stopped note sliding up a whole tone

# score: (time s, instrument, pitch, duration s, velocity 0-1, pan -1..1[, gain])
mix = S.render([
    (0.0, 'piano',   'D4', 1.0, .70, -.2),
    (0.0, 'cellos',  'D3', 4.0, .55,  .2),
    (0.5, 'violins', 'A4', 3.5, .50,  .3),
    dict(t=1.0, inst='harp', pitch='F#5', dur=1, vel=.6, pan=-.4),
    (2.0, 'gong', None, None, .5, 0),              # unpitched: pitch is the variant name or None
], dur=8)                                           # → (N,2) float32, limited per channel automatically above 0.95
mix = S.room(mix, size=.45, mix=.18)                # simple convolution reverb (optional)
sf.write('cue.wav', mix, SR)
```

> Calling `note()/hit()/pluck()` on their own gives **mono float32 @48k**, length ≈ `dur + release`; place it into a stereo buffer with `sfx.add(buf, x, t, gain, pan)`.

---

## 2. Using sampler.py

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `load(name)` | Loads an instrument by name (lazy + cached; the first call reads only the index, samples are read from disk when used). Returns an `Inst`; `print` shows range / velocity layers / variants |
| `note(inst, pitch, dur, vel=.8, release=None, attack=0, var=None)` | Single note. `pitch` can be `'C#4'` `'Db3'` `'Bb-1'` or a midi number (**C4=60**; fractions allowed = microtones). `dur` = how long the note is held; `release` = release time in seconds after the note stops (default per instrument); `attack>0` adds a fade-in for string pads |
| `hit(inst, name_or_index=None, vel=.8, dur=None)` | Unpitched hit. Variant names can be given as a prefix / without underscores (`'kick'`→`kick_drum_left`, `'hihat_open'`); an integer = the n-th variant (`hit('timpani', 2)` = the 3rd drum); `dur` truncates (with a 30 ms fade-out). Also works on pitched instruments: `hit('piano','A3')` plays the whole natural decay |
| `chord(inst, pitches, dur, vel, strum=0)` | Chord (mono); `strum>0` delays each note in turn (arpeggio / strum) |
| `render(events, dur=None, master=True)` | Score → stereo. Events are tuples `(t, inst, pitch, dur, vel, pan[, gain])` or dicts (may carry `release`/`attack`/`var`) |
| `room(x, size=.5, mix=.2, predelay=.015, damp=.5)` | Convolution reverb with a decorrelated exponentially decaying noise IR; `size` 0–1 → RT60 0.4–3.4 s; returns (N,2) of the same length |
| `credits(names)` | From the list of instruments you used, generates the end-credit CREDITS lines (the required CC BY wording + CC0 acknowledgements) |
| `info(name=None)` / `instruments(fam=None)` | Prints an overview / lists names (`fam` takes 弦乐 strings / 木管 woodwinds / 铜管 brass / 打击 percussion / 键盘 keyboards / 拨弦 plucked / 民族 folk) |
| `midi(p)` / `hz(p)` / `name(m)` / `seed(n)` | Note-name utilities; `seed` fixes the round-robin randomness (same call order → same result) |
| `build_index(names=None, force=False)` | Rescans the samples and rebuilds `index.json` (only needed if samples were swapped or added; ~15 s; needs librosa: `requirements-dev.txt`) |

**What it does behind the scenes**
- **Sample selection**: weighs both "closest to the target note" and "closest velocity layer" (cost = semitone distance + 4×velocity difference, with a small extra penalty for transposing up); multiple round-robins in the same cell rotate randomly, avoiding the machine-gun effect.
- **Transposition**: `soxr` HQ resampling (which also converts 44.1k to 48k). Keep transposition within ±4 semitones (samples are usually every 2–3 semitones, so the default stays within that range). Notes outside the sampled range still sound, but the timbre turns "cartoonish".
- **Velocity**: multi-layer instruments pick the layer first, then fine-tune ±4 dB within the layer; single-layer instruments scale gain by velocity and slightly darken the highs when played softly (real instruments are darker when played softly).
- **Long-note extension** (the `sustained, extendable` type): when `dur` exceeds the recording's length, grains of 0.4–1 s are taken at random from the recording's stable section, **aligned by cross-correlation at the fundamental period**, then spliced with 100 ms raised-cosine crossfades, and each grain's level is matched to the stable-section mean, so there is no hard cut and no looping "hum" periodicity. FreePats' accordion/bagpipe come with loop points; their loop regions are used directly.
- **Note-off**: after `dur`, an exponential decay over `release` (-60 dB) + 5 ms to zero; decaying instruments (piano, pizzicato, marimba…) decay naturally before `dur`, and when `dur` arrives they are "damped" over the release time. For glockenspiel/tubular bells/gong and the like, if you want them to ring on, write a long `dur` or a large `release`.
- **Level**: every instrument is already normalised from measurements of its recordings (sustained by the RMS of the loudest 0.4 s window, decaying by a 0.1 s window, percussion by each variant's peak), so at `vel=.8` the instruments are roughly equally loud (within ±6 dB). Balance directly with `vel`/`gain` when writing the score.
- **Pitch calibration**: every sample in the index has its fundamental measured with yin. In many VSCO/VCSL folders the file names are **an octave lower** than the actual pitch (e.g. `VlnEns_susVib_A2` is actually A3), while Karoryfer's erhu/bass file names are **an octave higher**: all of this is corrected automatically from the measurements (`octave_fix` in index.json), and samples off equal temperament by 8–80 cents are fine-tuned to equal temperament (Salamander uses its official Retuned table). **Just write the actual pitch.**

---

## 3. Using pluck.py (physically modelled plucked strings)

```python
P.pluck(preset, pitch, dur=None, vel=.8, **kw)   # → mono float32 @48k; dur=None lets it decay out naturally
P.strum(preset, pitches, dur, vel=.8, spread=.025, up=False)   # strum / arpeggio
```

| Preset | Description | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `guqin` | guqin | Silk strings, long sustain (~7 s), low-frequency body resonance; supports stopped-note slides with `bend` and yin-nao (吟猱) vibrato with `vib`, **silk-string friction noise is added automatically while sliding**; `harmonic=True` = harmonics (pure, bell-like) |
| `pipa` | pipa | Bright plectrum attack, decay ~2.5 s; `trem=12~16` = lunzhi (轮指, rolled-finger tremolo) |
| `shamisen` | shamisen | Plectrum + skin slap + **sawari buzz from the string touching the bridge** (`buzz` 0–1, `thr` adjustable; measured spectral centroid of the sustain 1.5k→2.0k Hz) |
| `koto` | koto (Japanese zither) | `bend` can do oshide (押手, pressing the string to raise the pitch) |
| `banjo` | banjo | Drum-head resonance, fast decay, stiff steel strings |
| `acoustic_guitar` | steel-string folk guitar | Pair with `strum()` for strumming |
| `nylon_guitar` | nylon-string guitar | Warm (sampled version: `guitar_nylon`) |
| `upright_bass_pizz` | double bass pizzicato | Dull fingertip thump + low-frequency body (sampled version: `jazz_bass`, more realistic) |
| `harp` | harp | Plucked at the string's midpoint, warm (sampled version: `harp`) |
| `kalimba` | kalimba | Modal synthesis: tine partials 1 : 5.93 : 16.6 + fingernail click + resonator box (sampled version: `kalimba`) |
| `music_box` | music box | Modal synthesis: comb-tooth partials 1 : 6.27 : 17.55, slight beating between paired teeth, mechanical "tick", short metallic decay |

Common keywords:
- `bend=[(t, semitones), ...]` piecewise-linear pitch envelope (relative to `pitch`); `glide=(target pitch, seconds)` glides to a note; `vib=(Hz, depth in semitones, start s)` vibrato / yin-nao
- `trem=Hz` lunzhi / yaozhi (轮指/摇指, tremolo: repeated plucks, velocity slightly randomised); `harmonic=True` harmonics
- Override physical parameters: `t60` (seconds for the fundamental to decay to -60 dB), `damp` (0–0.9, higher = darker), `pos` (pluck position 0–0.5, smaller = brighter), `bright`, `buzz`/`thr`, `bmix` (body proportion), `noise`, `release`

```python
# a guqin phrase: open string → stopped note sliding up → yin vibrato → harmonic
buf = np.zeros((int(8 * SR), 2), np.float32)
add(buf, P.pluck('guqin', 'D3', 2.5, .75), 0.0)
add(buf, P.pluck('guqin', 'A3', 3.0, .7, bend=[(0, 0), (.6, 0), (1.1, 2)], vib=(4.5, .2, 1.5)), 1.2)
add(buf, P.pluck('guqin', 'D5', 3.0, .6, harmonic=True), 4.0, .8, .2)
# pipa lunzhi tremolo + shamisen
add(buf, P.pluck('pipa', 'E4', 1.5, .7, trem=14), 0, .7, -.3)
add(buf, P.pluck('shamisen', 'C4', .6, .8, buzz=.7), 2, .8, .3)
```

## 6. Picking instruments by style (quick reference)

| The feel you want | Suggested combination |
|---|---|
| Orchestral / epic / documentary | `violins` `violas` `cellos` `contrabass` as the bed (`attack=.3~.8` fade-in) + `horn` `trombone` `tuba` + `timpani` `gran_cassa` `sus_cymbal:roll` `gong`; for light, brisk passages use `violins_spic` `cellos_pizz` `flute_stac` |
| Fairy tale / gentle / handmade | `glockenspiel` `celesta→glockenspiel` `pluck:music_box` `kalimba` `harp` `vibraphone` `hand_chimes` `ukulele` `guitar_nylon` + `clarinet` `flute` |
| Chinese | Samples: `erhu` `dan_tranh` (as guzheng) `dan_tranh_trem` (yaozhi tremolo) `gong2:small` `frame_drum` `log_drum` `woodblock`; modelled: `pluck:guqin` (with slides/harmonics) `pluck:pipa` (lunzhi tremolo); there are no dizi/xiao samples, use `flute` `recorder` `ocarina` instead |
| Japanese | `pluck:shamisen` `pluck:koto` + `flute`/`recorder` (in place of shakuhachi) + `gran_cassa` `frame_drum:large` `toms:low_mallet` (there is no CC0/CC BY taiko; layer these to build one) |
| Jazz / café | `piano` `jazz_bass` `alto_sax` `tenor_sax` `trumpet_mute` `vibraphone_hard` + `drum_kit:ride` `drum_kit:hihat` `snare2:taps` `claps` |
| Retro / old film / saloon | `honky_tonk` `upright` `accordion` `harmonica` `banjo` `clarinet` `tuba_stac` `strumstick` |
| Baroque / court | `harpsichord` `organ_soft` `recorder` `violin` `cellos` `oboe` `bassoon` |
| Church / sacred | `organ` `organ_pedal` `tubular_bells` `hand_chimes` `vibraphone_bowed` + a long `room(size=.8)` |
| Pop / upbeat | `drum_kit` `electric_bass` `electric_guitar` `piano` `glockenspiel` `claps` `shaker` `tambourine` |
| World / folk | `world_perc` (cajón/bongo/darbuka/castanets/shaker) `cajon` `conga` `mbira` `hang` `bagpipe` `pluck:banjo` `guitar_nylon` |
| Cold / ethereal / sci-fi | `vibraphone_bowed` `glass` `hang` `sus_cymbal:bow` `violins_trem` (low velocity) + `room(size=.9, mix=.35)` |

---

## 7. Known issues / cautions

- **`organ` (all stops out) includes the 16′**: the measured fundamental is an octave below the key name (pyin measures D3 for key D4); this is the organ's natural weight. If you want "key name = actual pitch", use `organ_soft`. `organ_pedal` pitches are given as measured.
- **Tubular bells `tubular_bells`**: a tubular bell's "strike tone" is a virtual pitch (the missing fundamental of partials 4/5/6 in the ratio 2:3:4); checked against the spectrum and correct, but pyin reports it an octave/fifth high, which is normal.
- **Timpani `timpani`**: only 5 drums (main vibration mode measured from the spectrum at about F2, B2, D3, E3, G3); `note('timpani', X)` transposes from the nearest drum; the most natural use is `hit('timpani', 'drum1'...)` or writing only notes between F2 and G3.
- **Hang `hang`**: the original instrument is in D minor (A3 D4 E4 F4 G4 A4 C5 D5 etc.); it sounds best on its own notes; other notes are transposed, and the overtones shift with them.
- **`tenor_sax` (vibrato version) has a slow attack**: for short notes use `tenor_sax_stac`/`tenor_sax_nv`; the `contrabass` sustained recordings contain real bow-change swells (about once every 2.3 s).
- **Long-note extension** has been tested at the 25 s scale: the extended section's level differs from the original recording's median by <1 dB, and level jumps between adjacent 0.1 s windows are mostly ≤3 dB (violin section/sax swing up to ~6 dB because of their own vibrato). For extremely long (>1 minute) sustained notes, retrigger in segments or overlap them with an `attack` fade-in.
- **Missing instruments**: no CC0/CC BY licensed samples were found for **taiko, a Chinese gong-and-drum set (big drum/cymbals/small gong as a full set), celesta, music box samples, acoustic steel-string guitar samples, dizi/xiao/shakuhachi** (Floe/SCC taiko is CC BY-SA, so it is excluded under the licence policy). Substitutes: taiko→`gran_cassa`+`frame_drum`+`toms:low_mallet`; gong→`gong`/`gong2:small`; celesta→`glockenspiel` (low velocity); music box→`pluck:music_box`; steel-string guitar→`pluck:acoustic_guitar`/`strumstick`.
- Files missing from the download: the FreePats ukulele's `chuck.wav` (muted strum) was restored with 7-Zip; nothing else is missing.
- The first call to `pluck` JIT-compiles (numba, ~0.5 s, result cached in `core/audio/__pycache__`); `sampler` takes ~10 ms the first time it reads a sample, then serves it from the memory cache (transposition results are cached too).
- Stereo: samples are mixed down to mono when read (one uniform interface); spatial feel comes from `pan` + `room()`.

---

## 8. Self-checks done (no listening was possible: everything rests on data)

**What was verified**
1. **Pitch**: every sample of all 97 sampled instruments had its fundamental measured with yin and written into `index.json`; the octave conventions of the file names were corrected by an octave-consistency vote (VSCO/VCSL mostly +12, Karoryfer −12, timpani from the main spectral vibration mode). The first note of 61 instruments was **rendered on its own and spot-checked with librosa.pyin: 59/61 within ±50 cents, passing ones with median deviation +3.7 cents and maximum 16 cents**; both "failures" are known and checked: tubular bells (virtual pitch; the 2:3:4 spectral partials confirm the strike tone is right) and `organ` (16′ stop, fundamental an octave low). Spot-checking the same 61 first notes directly in the finished mix: 57/61 pass; the other 4 (glockenspiel, tubular bells, erhu, banjo) were disturbed by the previous instrument's decay or are virtual pitches, and are all correct when rendered alone / checked against the spectrum (glockenspiel rendered alone: spectral peak = D6 +12 cents).
2. **Physical modelling**: 11 presets × 2–3 pitches all hit by pyin (within ±1 cent); the pyin trace of the guqin `bend` matches the setting (0.8→1.4 s sliding from 50 to 52); harmonic pitches correct; pipa lunzhi measured at 13.3 per second (set to 14); shamisen sawari on/off spectral centroid of the sustain 2030 Hz / 1500 Hz; decay times guqin≈4.3 s, pipa≈2.1 s, shamisen≈0.9 s, banjo≈1.0 s (T60 extrapolated from -30 dB).
3. **Finished-mix numbers**: 85.5 s, 48 kHz stereo, no NaN/Inf, peak −2.0 dBFS, 0 clipped samples; median 0.5 s RMS −24 dBFS.
4. **Long-note extension**: violin section/cello section/flute/trumpet/horn/clarinet/oboe/accordion/bagpipe/erhu/sax/organ rendered as 14–25 s long notes; the extended sections have no silent holes and their level matches the original recording (see the figures in the item above).
5. **Every instrument** has actually been loaded and rendered once (no exceptions, no NaN), every percussion variant hit once, and peaks normalised per variant to ~0.4.

**What could not be verified**
- Whether the subjective timbre is "convincing", whether the mix sounds good, whether velocity-layer switching is smooth, whether the extension splices have audible phase/timbre jumps: these can only be judged indirectly from data. Listen with your own ears the first time you use them (one small motif per instrument is enough).
- The "folk flavour" of the physical models (the guqin's loose, deep tone, the shamisen's sawari texture) was tuned only by physical parameters and spectral trends, never compared by ear with real recordings.
- Microtones, and the timbre of notes transposed more than ±6 semitones beyond the sampled range.

---

## 9. Directory layout

```
core/audio/
  sampler.py            sampled-instrument engine (section 2 of this file)
  pluck.py              physically modelled plucked strings + modal synthesis (section 3)
  instruments/
    index.json          pitch/velocity/level index (rebuildable with build_index())
    vsco2ce/            VSCO 2 CE selection (strings/woodwinds/brass/percussion/upright piano/pipe organ)  395 MB
    vcsl/               VCSL selection (harp/vibraphone/tubular bells/marimba/harpsichord/sax/harmonica/đàn tranh/percussion…) 271 MB
    salamander/         Salamander Grand Piano V3 (5 velocity layers, FLAC 48k/24bit)  218 MB
    freepats/           FreePats CC0 packs + MuldjordKit (CC BY 4.0)  397 MB
    karoryfer/          erhu / Sneakybass / Weresax  74 MB
```

Source links: VSCO 2 CE https://github.com/sgossner/VSCO-2-CE · VCSL https://github.com/sgossner/VCSL · Salamander https://freepats.zenvoid.org/Piano/acoustic-grand-piano.html · FreePats https://freepats.zenvoid.org/ · Karoryfer https://github.com/sfzinstruments (aliexpress-erhu / karoryfer.sneakybass / karoryfer.weresax)

Availability: the sample libraries must be downloaded first (`sh tools/fetch.sh instruments <lib>`, see the top of this file). When a library that hasn't been downloaded is used, `sampler` raises an error naming the command to run. `sampler.py` needs only the core-tier Python packages; `pluck.py` needs numba (`setup.sh deps music`).

# Style Name — Style Prompt

> One or two sentences: what the medium is and what it does on screen. No demo title, no story.
> References (grammar only): films, artists or traditions to learn the grammar from, and what to take from each. Never copy their characters, layouts, typefaces or music, and never name them in the film.

<!--
How to fill this template (delete this comment):
- This file holds only what stays true for EVERY film in this style: look, material, colour logic, type, motion quality,
  camera vocabulary, sound palette, the medium's native moves and pitfalls. 6–11 KB.
- No story, arc, beat-by-beat shot table, prescribed opening or ending, score arc, BPM or key, demo durations, demo palette or props, end card or sign-off.
  All of that goes to DEMO.md.
- A number measured in the demo becomes a rule here ("the subject fills ≥ 1/3 of the frame"); the demo's actual value
  can stay as an example in DEMO.md.
- Write rules, not history. "Pitfalls" are pitfalls of the medium, not of one demo prop.
- Section numbers are fixed: other guides refer to them.
-->

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

What makes a frame read as this style in one glance (3–5 defining traits). Then the styles it is easily confused with and the line between them ("not a keynote, not a blueprint, not a product render").

## 2. Materials & rendering

The physical medium and how code imitates it: surfaces, marks, layers, edges, texture, light. Name the rendering model (layers, blend modes, noise, stepping of marks). Say which effects must be procedural and anchored to the world, and which live in screen space.

## 3. Colour logic

Rules, not a palette: how many hues, what the neutral ground is, what the accent is reserved for, how values are ordered, what may never be coloured. Give one example palette at most, marked as an example.

## 4. Type & subtitles

Typefaces (licence-free), roles (title, subtitle, micro data), sizes as ranges, how subtitles belong to the world of the style (inscription, caption, HUD plate…), reading-time rule: hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s).

## 5. Motion quality

Frame rate and stepping (on ones / twos, what boils), easing families, weight, jitter, how things appear and disappear. What never moves.

## 6. Camera grammar

A vocabulary, not a route: the moves this medium does well, what each expresses, and a few kinds of moment it can serve. Opening and ending come from the topic.

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| e.g. slow lateral pan | … | a journey; a list; time passing |
| e.g. locked frame | … | a decision; a reveal; reading time |
| e.g. push-in | … | tension; the one detail that matters |

No row names the single move for an opening, a climax or an ending. If the demo's route is worth keeping, it goes to DEMO.md "Shots". Framing rules that always hold (subject size, safe areas, where text lives). Allowed and forbidden transitions.

## 7. Sound palette

Instruments and timbres, articulations, tuning or mode families, foley materials (what the style's matter sounds like), ambience, silence as a tool (what it may contain, how it is cut), mix character (ducking, loudness −14 LUFS), voice character. A technique may be written as one option ("divide the beat to accelerate instead of changing tempo"). No score arc, no section sequence, no BPM or key: those are the demo's and go to DEMO.md "Score structure".

## 8. Native moves

A menu of moments only this medium can do: use the ones your story needs. For each: what it is, how to build it, and **fits content like…** with three or more examples unlike the demo.

- **Move name.** What it does on screen. *Fits content like:* a …; a …; a ….

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

Mistakes that come from the medium itself, each with its fix. Pitfalls tied to one demo prop go to DEMO.md.

## 10. Engine

Which files in `demo/` hold reusable recipes (engine, rig, compositor, sampler set-up), their main functions and parameters, and a minimal example that draws something that is not in the demo. Point to the code; don't restate it.

## 11. Variation space

What the agent decides for each film (structure, characters, opening, ending, camera path, pacing, palette within the colour logic). Then, one line each and all far from the demo: **three structures**, **three openings** and **three endings**, to show the range.

Scene styles (a practical scene whose demo reads its words from `demo/content.json`) add here their **use cases** as information-order grammar: for each job, the order in which information arrives and how long each layer stays on screen. Swapping `content.json` is a technical check of the engine, not a way to make a film.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

# Archive Light Table — our demo

One example among many. Don't reuse its story, arc, shots, props or timings.

Demo: *Two Seconds Short* 《差两秒》 (40.0 s) · `archive-lighttable.mp4` · source in [`demo/`](demo/)

The Wright brothers' flights of 17 December 1903 on a light table, told through five Library of Congress items: two glass negatives, a telegram, a newspaper clipping, and a third negative as a prop. It is an unofficial film about a real event, made only from public-domain scans. Chinese on screen, English narration, bilingual subtitles (Chinese line above, English below). Every fact and its source is in [`demo/FACTS.md`](demo/FACTS.md).

## Story & structure

Logline: the telegram said the longest flight lasted 57 seconds, and the next day's paper printed it; the glass negatives and the Library's record say 59.

Arc: the claim (the table switches on; a loupe lands on Orville's telegram; inside the lens the lines light up and "57" lifts out as a reading) → the echo (the camera rises and glides to the Dayton Herald clipping, where the same sentence is underlined and its 57 ringed) → the evidence, which is also the emotional peak (the loupe lands on the first-flight negative, the negative turns positive inside the lens, the camera falls through the lens into the photograph, and the Flyer separates from the horizon and drifts forward; 12 s, 120 ft) → the measurement (the fourth-flight negative: a ruler laid on the ground plane from the camera to the tiny machine on the horizon; 852 ft, 59 s) → the verdict (57 and 59 side by side, held still 2.7 s, then 57 is struck: "差 2 秒") → the ending (pull back to the whole table; every object's tag flies into one archive index; end card).

Native moves spent: *the line lights up* on the telegram and the clipping; *negative to positive under the loupe* and *into the photograph* for the first flight (the signature, at the peak); *measuring on the photograph* for the fourth flight; *two records, held side by side* for the verdict; *the table becomes the index* for the ending.

## Shots

One continuous camera over one table; framing changes by zoom and by passing through the loupe. Times in seconds.

| # | Time | Shot | Camera | Native move / note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.0–1.3 | the dark table flickers on (0.0, 0.17, 0.42, 0.55; steady at 0.67); the telegram fills two thirds of the frame, the clipping at the bottom edge | glide toward the telegram with a 4° roll that levels it | the starter clicks and hum are the first sounds |
| 2 | 1.3–2.0 | the loupe drops onto the telegram (scale 1.35 → 1, shadow tightening) | settles | glass clack on the beat |
| 3 | 2.0–3.3 | push into the lens: the rim passes the frame while the view inside widens to the whole message | zoom 0.31 → 1.5 | the date line lights at 2.67 |
| 4 | 3.3–9.3 | inside the telegram: "Success four flights …" lights at 4.0, "… longest 57 seconds …" at 7.33, each with an underline; the rest of the paper dims; 57 is ringed at 8.0 and a reading card "电报 · 最长一次 57 秒" draws out to the right | slow track along the lines, then a push onto 57 | reading |
| 5 | 9.3–11.3 | rise out of the lens; the loupe lifts at 10.33; the card stays on screen until 11.4 | zoom out and glide down-right | a ring stays on the telegram's 57 |
| 6 | 11.3–13.3 | the Dayton Herald clipping: "longest time in air was 57 seconds." lights and underlines at 12.0, its 57 ringed at 12.33; a caption plate "1903.12.18 / 代顿先驱报" held still on the right | push in with a 4° roll | the echo |
| 7 | 13.3–14.7 | glide to the first-flight negative; crop corners (the 16:9 frame the photograph will open to) | glide and settle | the loupe lands at 14.67 |
| 8 | 14.7–16.0 | inside the lens the negative; a develop front from the centre turns it positive (15.0–15.8); readout "×2.5 负像 → 正像" | hold | |

| 10 | 18.0–22.7 | the photograph in depth: the Flyer (its own layer) drifts 125 px forward and up against the horizon; the sand swells under a dolly; wind over the dunes; labels "第一次飞行 / 12 秒 · 120 英尺 · 上午 10:35", "威尔伯·莱特", "快门：John T. Daniels" | dolly (0.55) + lateral shift (260, −140) about the Flyer's depth | near-silence from 21.3: wind only |
| 11 | 22.7–24.7 | rise out of the photograph; glide over the 14 December plate to the fourth-flight negative | zoom out, glide right | |
| 12 | 24.7–26.3 | the loupe lands; push in; the positive already shows (the viewer stays switched on) | zoom 0.31 → 1.45 | |
| 13 | 26.3–30.0 | the ruler: from the bottom edge (the camera, the start) to the machine on the horizon, ticks every 100 ft crowding into perspective, labels 100 / 200 / 400; the reading counts 852 ft (lands 28.67) and 59 s (lands 30.0); "落地点" ringed | push toward the machine (0.62 → 1.3) with a ground-plane dolly | ticks on every 100 ft |
| 14 | 30.0–33.3 | two caption cards: the telegram's own line (a crop of the scan) "57 秒", the record's wording "852 feet covered in 59 seconds." "59 秒"; held still 2.67 s; silence from 32.8 | locked | comparison held before the verdict |
| 15 | 33.3–35.9 | 57 struck in signal orange, "差 2 秒" | locked, then the rise begins under the cards at 35.0 | the strike lands on low D after the silence |
| 16 | 35.9–40.0 | pull back to the whole light table in its frame on the dark desk; five tags fly into "档案索引" (the two 57s struck); end card at 36.33 | zoom to 0.094, roll to level | scale reveal |

## Score structure

90 BPM, 4/4; every key action on a beat or half-beat (`demo/tools/cuecheck.mjs`), except the two breaths (17.6, 32.8), which sit just before their downbeats by design. B minor turning to D major.

| Section | Time | Palette | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light | 0–2.7 | piano D5 with the light; hum and starter clicks | |
| Telegram | 2.7–10.7 | felt piano broken chords in eighths, Bm–G–D–A; a paper sweep and a glass ring on each lit line; cellos D3 and violas A3 enter under the 57 | |
| Clipping | 10.7–13.3 | the same broken chords, quieter (Bm, G) | an echo |
| First flight | 13.3–23.6 | D at the glide; strings swell from the develop (attack 1.6 s), piano climbs D4 → A5 in eighths and a noise riser rises through the push; everything is cut at 17.6; at 18.0 the full D chord (piano D2–A4, strings, contrabass D2, glass D6, a soft cymbal), then a falling line A4–F♯4–D4–E4–F♯4 | wind and surf replace the hum inside the photograph |
| Measure | 26.3–32.8 | piano eighths on an A-major pedal, getting slightly louder; cellos A3 and violas E4 underneath; ticks every 100 ft; glass A5 at 852, E6 at 59 | acceleration by density, not tempo |
| Verdict | 32.8–33.3 | silence (hum only) | |
|  | 33.3 | pen stroke, piano D2/D3/A3, glass D6, soft timpani D3 | |
| End | 35.7–40.0 | the theme in D (F♯4–A4–D5–C♯5–A4), ticks as index rows land; the final D chord with strings and bowed vibraphone at 36.33 | |

Mix (in `mix.py`): music about 11 dB under the voice before ducking, ducked a further ~5 dB while the narrator speaks; foley 9 dB under the voice, beds 24 dB under; a 38 Hz high-pass on everything but the voice; a master limiter keeps the peak-to-RMS ratio near 11.5 dB so `mux.sh` can reach −14 LUFS under −1.2 dBTP.

## Palette & props

- Table #F7F9FB with a brushed-aluminium frame and a dark desk (#0E0F11); ink #15171A; signal orange #FF5A1F; caption plates rgba(14,15,17,0.74).
- Props (all Library of Congress, true scale, 5000 world units = 7 in): telegram (LC-USZ62-65459 / mcc.061), Dayton Herald clipping (LC-USZ62-70686), first-flight negative (LC-DIG-ppprs-00626), fourth-flight negative (LC-DIG-ppprs-00629), 14 December negative (LC-DIG-ppprs-00610).
- The loupe: 2.5×, lens radius 1000 world units (≈ 1.4 in).
- Narrator: Kokoro `bm_george`, speeds 0.92–1.0.

## End card

Over the pulled-back table, bottom left: 差两秒 (Noto Serif SC), *Two Seconds Short*, a signal-orange rule, `ARCHIVE LIGHT TABLE` 档案灯台, `LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5`; the archive index on the right. 3.7 s. The "LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5" sign-off belongs to this library's demo only; a user's film carries no LemoLab credit and no copy of this card.

## Build notes

```
demo/
  build.sh          one command: (FETCH) scans + textures + fonts → voice → speech check → cues → cue grid →
                    video → mix → master → .srt → subtitle widths → readcheck → poster + style frame
  index.html        two canvases (WebGL2 picture, 2D marks), fonts
  film.js           the table, camera keys, the three dives, the shader, every mark, readouts, index, end card, subtitles
  timeline.js       beats, key actions, narration, subtitle cues (single source; tools/export.mjs → out/timeline.json, out/cues.json)
  mix.py            score, foley, beds, voice, mix → out/mix.wav + out/stems/
  tools/            prep.py (masks, layers, fill), fonts.py, sru.py (LoC catalogue lookups), export.mjs,
                    cuecheck.mjs, subcheck.mjs
  sources/          the Library of Congress catalogue records (MARCXML) behind FACTS.md
  assets/           raw/ (downloads), tex/ (textures the page reads)
  FACTS.md, CREDITS, stills/styleframe.jpg
```

- `sh demo/build.sh` takes about 4 minutes on Apple silicon (the picture renders in about 40 s with 4 workers; the master pass is the slowest step). From a clean clone it first fetches what git does not hold: the fonts from Google Fonts (`tools/fonts.py`), the Kokoro model and the salamander, vsco2ce and vcsl sample libraries (`tools/fetch.sh`), and about 100 MB of Library of Congress scans, which `tools/prep.py` turns into textures (about 25 s). `FETCH=1` forces the fonts and scans again.
- Checks it runs: `asr_check.py` with `small.en` (two lines carry an `asr` field: Whisper writes "17th, 1903" for the spoken date and hears "four flights" as "for flights"), the cue grid, subtitle single-line widths measured with the real fonts (widest 648 px against 1500 px), `readcheck.mjs`.
- Demo-specific pitfalls: loc.gov item pages sit behind a Cloudflare challenge, so the catalogue records come from the Library's SRU server (`lx2.loc.gov:210/lcdb`) and the files from `tile.loc.gov`; in the first-flight plate the sky can be unmixed exactly against a smooth membrane, but the sand cannot, so below the horizon only strong marks are cut (lower wing, skids, struts; a vertical-line filter catches thin struts) and the rest stays on the ground; the fourth-flight scan is low in contrast and gets its own levels in the positive; the clipping is a low-resolution copy, so the camera never pushes past about 0.66 zoom on it.

# Archive Light Table — Style Prompt

> Real archive objects (glass negatives, slides, letters, telegrams, clippings, drawings) lie on a cool, backlit light table. A loupe comes down on one of them, and inside the glass the object comes alive: a negative turns positive, a line of type lights up, a number lifts off the page, a photograph opens into depth. Precise catalogue numbers, dates and readings are pinned to the objects. Clean, modern and quiet, with no vintage filter.
> References (grammar only): archive documentaries that push into still photographs; visual investigations that annotate real imagery (one line, one reading, one source per screen); product macro films (glass edges, transmitted light). Copy none of their layouts, typefaces, shots or music, and never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

- **The objects are real**: scans of public-domain or licensed archive items, at their true proportions, with their real damage (broken corners, emulsion edges, folds, pencil marks). Nothing in them is drawn or generated.
- **Light comes from below**: the table glows a near-white cool grey; film and glass transmit it, paper glows warm at its edges, opaque things read darker than the table.
- **The loupe is the camera's door**: every dive into an object goes through a loupe that lands on it. The inside of the lens is where the object changes state.
- **Catalogue truth**: every object carries its real identifier, date and title from its holder; numbers on screen come from the record.
- **One signal colour** for marks, readings and anchors; everything else is the archive's own greys and paper tones.

**Sources and licences.** Open collections with masters and catalogue records: the Library of Congress (files on `tile.loc.gov`; records from its SRU server `lx2.loc.gov:210/lcdb` when loc.gov pages are blocked), Smithsonian Open Access (CC0), the Rijksmuseum (CC0), NARA, Europeana (check each item's rights statement). CC0, public domain and CC BY (credited) are fine. "No known restrictions", CC BY-SA and other terms are not CC0: name the terms to the user and ask. For brand history, ask the user for their scans, archive numbers and right to use them. Never stand a generated image in for an archive object. Keep a `FACTS.md` in the project folder (claim, source URL, quoted wording, or how a figure was derived) and deliver it with the film.

Not Halftone Dossier (no newsprint dots, no aged-paper grade), not Satellite Briefing (objects on a table, not the ground from orbit), not Data Storytelling (no charts; the numbers live on the objects), not a keynote (no slides or header bars).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **One world, one camera**: every object is a textured quad on the table with a centre, rotation and scale (texture px → world units at true size). The camera is a 2D centre, zoom and roll; the table and every mark go through the same world → screen function.
- **The light table**: an emissive surface (≈ 0.97 white, slightly cool), soft falloff, diffuser noise, an aluminium frame and a dark desk beyond. It can be switched off (ambient ≈ 0.04) and flicker on.
- **Glass negatives**: transmission from the scan's positive, `T = 0.035 + 0.9 · (1 − pos)^1.25`, with a warm silver-gelatin tint; the emulsion mask comes from the scan (white margin touching the border = no glass), so broken corners show the table. Dust and scratches are procedural, anchored to the table.
- **Paper**: backlit, its colour is transmission (paper tone × light); lit lines get darker ink and brighter paper; unlit text can dim to bring one line forward.
- **The loupe**: inside the lens each pixel maps back to the table through the magnification (≈ 2.5×) with a pincushion term (k ≈ 0.16 at the rim), slightly different per RGB channel for colour fringes. Around it: a black ring with a bevel highlight and a clear acrylic skirt that refracts the table and glows at its foot. Landing and lifting, it scales by about 1.35× and casts a soft shadow.
- **The photograph space**: after the push the lens stops being a lens. A photo gains depth from a ground-plane nearness map (zero at the horizon, linear in the row below it), cut-out layers for upright subjects and a filled background; a dolly and a lateral shift drive parallax, and a subject layer may drift. Things left on the ground plane lean: centre the dolly between them.
- **Sampling**: all texture reads inside the branching lens code use explicit gradients (`textureGrad`), otherwise quads that cross a branch pick a wrong mip level and leave dashed seams.
- **Marks** live on a 2D canvas above the picture: hairlines 1.5–3 px, rings, crop corners, underlines, leaders. Table marks are clipped out under the loupe; marks inside a photograph use its forward mapping, parallax included.
- **Post**: a light vignette and fine moving grain (heavier inside photographs). No film damage, no sepia, no halftone.

## 3. Colour logic

- Neutral ground: the light table (near-white, cool) and the archive's own tones (silver greys, paper tans). Do not regrade the archive into a colour scheme.
- **One signal colour** (e.g. a signal orange) for marks, readings, anchors and the verdict; never as a fill behind pictures, never for decoration.
- Text is ink (near-black) on light areas and paper-white on dark caption plates; choose the contrast by the ground, never colour on colour.
- Positives inside the lens may be gently levelled (black and white points) so a weak scan reads; negatives stay as the glass gives them.

Example (our demo): table #F7F9FB, ink #15171A, signal #FF5A1F, caption plates rgba(14,15,17,0.74).

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Roles**: a monospace for identifiers, dates and readings (e.g. IBM Plex Mono, 17–34 px; readings 74–120 px); a sans for labels in the film's language (e.g. Noto Sans SC or Inter, 21–36 px); a serif only for titles and the one name a photograph carries (60–76 px). OFL, self-hosted, CJK subset when needed.
- **Labels attach to objects**: an anchor dot and ring, a vertical leader, then the text. A reading sits in a dark caption plate with a small label above and the source (the catalogue number or the original wording) below.
- **Subtitles** are a caption strip at the bottom centre, on a dark plate with a 3 px signal-coloured edge. If the film is bilingual, the film's language goes on top. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s).
- **Quote the source when you can**: a crop of the actual line, or the record's wording in quotation marks, beats a paraphrase.

## 5. Motion quality

- 24 fps on ones; every camera parameter on smooth monotone curves through keys (no overshoot, no stepping).
- The camera glides across the table, slows to let the loupe land, then pushes. Speed lives in the glides and pushes; holds are for reading.
- The loupe lands with a fast ease-out (≈ 0.4 s), lifts the same way. Lines draw on in 0.3–0.6 s; text wipes in from its leader side; numbers count up and land with the voice.
- What never moves: the archive's own content outside a photograph space, and the table itself.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| table glide (pan and roll) | surveying; moving to the next piece of evidence | a timeline of documents; a product family; an album |
| loupe landing + push into the lens | choosing one object; "look closer" | the claim; the key photograph; a signature |
| inside the lens: tracking along a line | reading | a letter, a ledger line, a caption, a spec |
| photograph space: dolly + parallax | being there | the event itself; the founding moment; the place |
| rise out of the lens | stepping back, the evidence noted | a transition; a summary |
| pull back to the whole table | scale; everything at once | an index, a timeline, a closing |

Framing: at a reading moment the subject fills at least a third of the frame height; readings and labels stay clear of the subtitle strip (bottom 140 px). Transitions are made by the loupe (land, push, rise, lift) and the glide; no cuts, fades to black or page turns between objects.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Ambience**: the light table's ballast hum (100 Hz and harmonics), starter clicks, room tone. Inside a photograph the hum gives way to that place's air.
- **Foley**: the loupe on glass (a clack with a high ring), paper sweeps for glides and lit lines, ticks for scales and counters, a pen stroke for a verdict, soft clicks as labels land.
- **Music**: restrained and small: a felt piano, a few strings, glass or bowed metal for the moments of seeing. Build by subdivision and register, not by drums. Leave real silences before a reveal or a verdict; the first sound after them should be the loupe, the place or the verdict.
- **Voice**: a calm narrator, short sentences that state what the object says. Music about 10 dB under the voice, ducked while it speaks; −14 LUFS.

## 8. Native moves

- **Negative to positive under the loupe.** A develop front spreads from the lens centre with a thin warm edge, turning the glass negative into its positive only inside the lens. *Fits content like:* a founder's portrait plate; a factory on a lantern slide; an X-ray film becoming the product inside.
- **The line lights up.** On paper inside the lens one line of type brightens while the rest dims, an underline draws under it, and one word or number lifts out into a reading card. *Fits content like:* a ledger entry; a patent claim; the first order on an invoice.
- **Into the photograph.** The lens rim grows past the frame while the view inside widens; the photograph gains layered depth and a subject drifts. *Fits content like:* the first shop front; a launch day crowd; an expedition camp.
- **Measuring on the photograph.** A ruler laid on the ground plane in perspective, with ticks that crowd toward the horizon and a counter that lands on the recorded figure, marked as a schematic when it is one. *Fits content like:* a race distance; a bridge span; a building's height.
- **Two records, held side by side.** Two caption cards, each with a crop of its source, held still until both are read before one is struck. *Fits content like:* a misprinted date; two versions of a founding story; specification against delivery.
- **The table becomes the index.** Pull back to the whole table; each object's tag flies into one list with its identifier and its reading. *Fits content like:* a company timeline; a collection catalogue; a product family.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Over-magnifying a weak scan**: keep the lens interior under about 1.5 screen px per scan px; choose items by scan size.
- **The loupe sweeping over empty table**: lay objects close together, land the loupe straight onto the object (drop in, don't slide in), and glide the camera over objects, not gaps.
- **Shear in the photograph space**: one depth map for a photo with people or machines in it tears them apart. Cut upright subjects into layers, fill behind them, and keep 2.5D moves small enough that the fill is barely seen.
- **Labels that scroll away**: a label on a moving table leaves the frame before it is read; hold the camera, or fix the caption on screen.
- **Vintage creep**: no sepia, no halftone, no paper-ageing overlay. The age is in the objects, not the grade.

## 10. Engine

- `demo/film.js`: `IT` (objects: centre, rotation, scale), `toW()` / `toT()` (texture ↔ world), `CAM` keys and `w2s()`, `dive()` (loupe point, land/lift times, lens interior as tracks), `shot(t)`, `int2s()` (photograph → screen for marks), the shader (`lightTable`, `paper`, `negative`, `parallax`, rim and skirt), the overlay (`annot`, `measure`, `compare`, `indexPanel`).
- `demo/tools/prep.py`: emulsion masks from scans, difference matting of a subject against a smooth sky, ground-only cuts, push-pull fill.
- Minimal example, not in the demo: put one 35 mm slide (`IT.slide = {c, r, k, size}`), a loupe landing with `dive(toW(IT.slide, p), t0, t1, keysS, keysC)`, and light one line with `band()`.
- **Extra packages and packs**: none beyond `setup.sh deps voice music` (numpy, scipy, Pillow, soxr are in the core tier). A score in this palette needs sample libraries: `sh tools/fetch.sh instruments salamander` (piano), `vsco2ce` (strings), `vcsl` (glass, bowed vibraphone). Anything else a film needs goes into a private venv or `node_modules` in the project folder, never into `$LIB/.venv`.

## 11. Variation space

The agent decides the objects, their order, the story, which native moves to spend and where, the camera path, the subject of the photograph space, and the signal colour.

- **Three structures**: a company's founding told as five objects in date order, each dive revealing one person; a single photograph explored in three dives (the place, the people, the date on the back); a before/after pair of plans and photographs of one building.
- **Three openings**: the table switching on in the dark; a loupe already on a plate, rising to reveal the table; a hand-written date on an envelope filling the frame.
- **Three endings**: the index of everything on the table; the last photograph held in depth with one line of text; the light table switching off, leaving one object glowing.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

# Art Deco — our demo

One example among many. Don't reuse its story, arc, shots, props or timings.

Demo: *Midnight at the Starlight Hotel* (58.4 s) · `art-deco.mp4` · source in [`demo/`](demo/)


The original brief for the demo: a 40–60 second film in the Art Deco style; the director decides story, shots, score, sound and titles.

## Story & structure

A bellboy, Pip, must carry a sealed letter to the rooftop before midnight on New Year's Eve 1930. A small, urgent errand in a grand place. A mechanical obstacle (the elevator is OUT OF ORDER) turns panic into resolve. A rising middle with a tempo change (the stairs = Charleston). A true silence before the climax (the clock hits XII, the band stops, the letter tumbles). The climax is counted light: twelve strikes of midnight = the twelve letters of THE STARLIGHT lighting one by one.

**The music is the plot:** the letter holds the band's new song; the theme is only heard in fragments until the conductor opens it, and the 13th beat is the first full statement. Echo at the end: the hero who looked up at a dark sign now stands inside the lit one; a button gag closes the loop (the elevator dings IN SERVICE — too late).

How the style's native powers were spent in this story:

| Native power | Demo use |
|---|---|
| The centre axis | Every transition is a door: the title arch splits open, stair doors burst, kitchen swing doors bang, elevator doors close into the end card. |
| Counted light | The bulb sign lights letter by letter, one per bell. |
| Machine symmetry | A Busby Berkeley overhead: fans opening on eighth notes become a sunburst, then lock into a clock face. Used as the release after the climax. |
| Dials & numbers | Floor indicator, clock face, floor medallions, year badge: floor 30, 11:55, 1930 carry the plot without narration. |
| Period radio | An announcer as narrator, moved through acoustic spaces (street horn → desk radio → stairwell PA → live mic) so the audience hears the hero getting closer to the source. |

The recipe we used to adapt it (for this demo): find the threshold (doors), the deadline (a clock), the counted reveal (a sign, floor numbers), and the thing the finale unlocks (a song).

## Shots

| Beat | Camera |
|---|---|
| Opening (3 s hook) | A single gold point explodes into rays and stepped arches; slow 6 % push. Title bar blooms on the orchestra hit. |
| Transition grammar | **Symmetric split**: the outgoing frame becomes two door leaves hinged at the edges that swing open from the seam (arch, stair doors, kitchen doors). The revolving door is its rotary cousin (glass wings wipe). The film closes with elevator doors sliding shut over the live shot. |
| Establishing | Extreme low-angle Cassandre tilt from the dark sign at the top of the tower down to the tiny hero on the street: goal, difficulty and the dark sign (the setup of the ending) in one move. |
| Obstacle | Medium on the plaque dropping; a slow push on the face during the silence while he straightens his cap. |
| Signature 1 | The stairwell as an **architectural section**: rise with him, pull out until the whole tower is a cutaway and he is a red dot with speed lines, push back in on the "30" floor medallion, match-cut to a spinning silver tray in the kitchen. |
| Silence | Insert of the tower clock's minute hand clicking to XII; the letter tumbling in slow motion past the dark letters. |
| Climax | Twelve bells: catch (ECU glove) → conductor (tear the seal, insert of the score, baton up) → low oblique of the sign as letters light one per strike → close-up as the last T lights behind the hero, gold light across his face. |
| Signature 2 | **Busby Berkeley**: an oblique high angle as 8 dancers open their fans one per eighth note, then straight overhead, 8-way mirrored and slowly rotating; the fans lock into a clock face with two gold hands at XII. |
| Scale reveal | Pull back from the sign to the whole tower, the city and fireworks (echoes the opening tilt). |
| Ending | Elevator doors slide shut over the live shot; the end card plaque sits on the closed doors. |

Performance beats: the elevator button pressed three times (once, twice, mash); the throw has a wind-up, release and a near-fall over the railing; the cap knocked off by a tray lands back on his head one bar later while he doesn't even look. In the opening the gold lines grow at the speed of the clarinet glissando (slow → fast), landing on the downbeat hit. After all letters are lit, a 16th-note chase runs across the whole sign.

## Score structure

- **Score first**: `timeline.js` is the single source of truth (116 BPM foxtrot → 16 beats accelerating to 138 BPM Charleston → stop → 12 bells on the 116 grid → the song in D♭). `tools/cuecheck.py` checks 53 picture sync points against `music/score.json` (max offset 0.5 ms).
- **Orchestration as used**: piano lead (Salamander), clarinet (low trill + two-octave glissando curtain-raiser), strings (tremolo bed, upward rushes), muted trumpet commentary ("wah-wah" on the plaque), brushes → sticks in the Charleston, walking pizz bass, tubular bells (B♭) for midnight, harp/piano glissandi for each fan, trombone + sax for the final chorus.
- **Planting the theme**: title = piano bar 1; street = muted trumpet tries two bars and is cut off; kitchen = the hero whistles the first four notes; finale = the full song.
- **Distance automation**: the band plays on the 30th floor, so it is low-passed at 2.5 kHz on the street, 1.2 kHz in the lobby (through the floor), opens up as he climbs, full-range and dry on the roof.
- **Announcer in five spaces** (Kokoro `bm_fable`): street horn (band-pass 320–3.8 kHz, soft drive, slap echo) → desk radio → stairwell PA (long reverb) → kitchen radio → live mic (full range). Heavy horn distortion made "five minutes to midnight" unintelligible in the full mix, so the drive was reduced.
- **Foley as used**: brass button click, bronze plaque clang + chain rattle, iron stair treads on eighth notes, marble heels, silver trays, wooden swing doors + spring twang, paper flutter, glove slap, knife-switch "chunk" + filament hum per letter, relay ticks for the chase, firework whistles.
- **Silences**: after "Out of order?!" only the lobby clock ticks twice (next sound: the Charleston snare); after the tower clock clicks to XII only wind and the fluttering letter (next sound: the first bell, the most important sound in the film); one beat of held breath after bell 12 (next: tutti).
- **J/L-cuts**: radio tuning noise before the arch opens; the echo of "Out of order?!" rolls up the stairwell; the kitchen radio starts during the stairwell; rooftop wind enters a bar before the kitchen doors; bell 12's tail rings into the tutti.
- Mix: music ducked ≈ −9 dB under voice (−6 dB under the live announcer), beds −6 dB; −14 LUFS, grain 3.

## Palette & props

- Ground: warm black `#0d0b09`, lacquer `#060504`; night sky `#0a0e16` → horizon emerald `#10231f`.
- Gold: `#6F5220` (shadow) → `#C9A24B` (base) → `#F3D98B` (light) → `#FFF4D2` (specular).
- Accents: burgundy `#8E1B2E` (the hero's uniform, the only large saturated area), emerald `#1D6B57` (fans, door panels, night), ivory `#F2E8D5` (the letter, gloves, carpet).
- Scenes: the lobby in one-point perspective with a mode-7 floor; the rooftop sign in two-point perspective from below with a tiny pinhole camera.
- Pip: 7 heads tall, tapered streamline body, faceted lacquer planes; silhouette marks: tilted pillbox cap + chin strap, a V of brass buttons, the sealed letter always in hand.
- Other props: the OUT OF ORDER plaque, the tower clock, the bulb sign THE STARLIGHT, the conductor and the score, waiters with silver trays, 8 dancers with emerald fans, fireworks.
- Reference stills (rebuilt by `build.sh`, same renderer as the film): [`demo/stills/modelsheet_v2.jpg`](demo/stills/modelsheet_v2.jpg), Pip's model sheet (turnaround on a 7-head scale, silhouette check, six expressions, key poses, palette swatches, the letter); [`demo/stills/kit_v2.jpg`](demo/stills/kit_v2.jpg), the component kit (title bar, numerals and clocks, sunburst, arch frames, patterns, bulb marquee, subtitle cards), each labelled with its engine call; style frames [`demo/stills/frame_v2_lobby.jpg`](demo/stills/frame_v2_lobby.jpg) (the one-point lobby with the mode-7 floor) and [`demo/stills/frame_v2_roof.jpg`](demo/stills/frame_v2_roof.jpg) (the bulb sign from below in two-point perspective).

## Titles & end card

- Subtitle card speaker icons: a gold ribbon mic for the announcer, a burgundy pillbox cap for the hero.
- Title: MIDNIGHT / AT THE STARLIGHT HOTEL in a gold title bar over the stepped arch, a 1930 diamond year badge, NEW YEAR'S EVE label.
- End card: a lacquer plaque on the closed elevator doors: title, ART DECO, LEMO-OPUSCAR, "LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5", asset credits. This sign-off belongs to this library's demo only; a user's film carries no LemoLab credit and no copy of this card.

## Build notes

```
styles/art-deco/demo/
  timeline.js      tempo grid + all sync points (single source of truth) → tools/dump_timeline.mjs → timeline.json
  engine/          deco.js (palette, gold, gline, airbrush, motifs, drawShape) · type.js (title bar, digits, badges, dial, clock, subtitle card)
                   bulbs.js (any text → bulb sign, lighting patterns) · cam.js (pinhole camera + card transforms)
  chars.js         Pip (FK rig, 4 views, 8 faces, pose library, run cycles), conductor, waiters, dancers, the letter
  scenes/          lobby.js (one-point + mode-7 floor, doors, plaque) · roof.js (two-point sign) · tower.js · stairs.js
  shots_*.js       one function per shot: shot(g, t)       film.js   shot list, transitions (split / revolve / close), subtitles
  frames.js        model sheet, component kit, style frames, ?scene=frames.shotTest&shot=<name>
  music/score.py   original score → score.wav + stems + score.json      mix.py   voices in 5 spaces + foley + beds + ducking
  tools/           cuecheck.py · subs.py · pitch.py · dump_timeline.mjs
```
1. Write the tempo grid and the cue table first; hand them to a music sub-agent and draw in parallel.
2. Build the engine and the hero model sheet, then one scene per location, then one function per shot. Review single shots with `?scene=frames.shotTest&shot=<name>`.
3. `sh demo/build.sh` rebuilds everything: timeline → TTS → pitch → whisper → score → cue check → mix → srt → render (≈15 s with 4 workers for 1401 frames) → mux (−14 LUFS, grain 3) → stills.
4. Review at 1 s intervals with `still.mjs --range 0:58:1` + `sheet.py`, then frame strips at 0.15–0.2 s for every key action.

Pitfalls tied to this demo's props:
- The first transition to the end card slid the elevator doors in over a flat brown "interior", which read as a blank frame; only the leaves are drawn now, closing over the live shot.
- The opening (one gold point on black) tripped `blackdetect`; the background sunburst wedges and glow were lifted.
- Pip at ¼ frame height in the bell shots was too small for the emotional peak; the last bell got a close-up.
- Three-digit hex turned the emerald fans blue-violet.

## Engine reference

All drawing is Canvas2D, deterministic in `t`. Import from `demo/engine/`.

**type.js**: `goldText(g, text, x, y, {size, font, track, sheen})` · `titleBar(g, text, cx, cy, {p, out, size, sub, wings})` (animated in/out) · `decoDigits(g, '11:59', x, y, size)` · `yearBadge(g, '1930', cx, cy, r, {p})` · `floorMedallion(g, '30', cx, cy, r, {sub})` · `dial(g, cx, cy, r, value, {labels})` (semicircle floor indicator, value 0..1) · `clockFace(g, cx, cy, r, {h, m, s, roman})` · `subtitleCard(g, text, {p, out, speaker:'radio'|'boy'})`.

**cam.js**: `makeCam({x, y, z, f, yaw, pitch, roll})` → `{P(X,Y,Z), scaleAt(X,Y,Z)}` · `cardTransform(g, cam, TL, TR, BL, w, h)` (map a flat card onto a 3D quad).

**chars.js** (demo characters): `drawFigure(g, {x, y, s, view:'side'|'q'|'front'|'back', face, ...pose})` · `POSES`, `FRONT_POSES`, `lerpPose`, `runCycle(phase)`, `runFront(phase)` · `drawDancer`, `drawDancerTop`, `envelope`, `clef`.

**The one colour.** To keep one element in its own colour, pass `color` — it is used for the fill, keyline and glow while everything else stays gold:

```js
import * as D from './engine/deco.js';
import * as B from './engine/bulbs.js';

// a warm-orange four-point light with a short cursor tail, drawn the Art Deco way
D.sunburst(g, 960, 540, { rays: 72, r1: 1400, mode: 'wedges' });
D.drawShape(g, D.starPts(960, 540, 120, .22), { color: '#D97757', halo: 1, trail: { ang: Math.PI, len: 420, n: 4 } });

// a bulb sign that lights letter by letter, in the same orange
const sign = B.buildSign('LEMO', { size: 260, spacing: 20 });
B.drawSign(g, sign, 560, 700, 1, { lit: B.litSequence(t, [0, .5, 1, 1.5], { chaseFrom: 2.5 }), color: '#D97757' });
```

# Art Deco — Style Prompt

> Black lacquer, engraved gold line and airbrushed geometry: a 1930s poster that moves. Every composition has a centre axis, transitions open or close along it, and light arrives as bulbs switching on one by one.
> References (grammar only): **A. M. Cassandre** posters (giant geometry, steep perspective, airbrush inside hard edges); **Chrysler Building / Rockefeller Center ornament** (setbacks, sunbursts, chevrons); **Busby Berkeley** overhead numbers overheads (human kaleidoscopes); **The Great Gatsby (2013) title sequence** (gold line drawing itself on black); **Gershwin-era symphonic jazz** (clarinet, piano, muted trumpet). Never copy a poster layout, a real building, a character, a typeface design or a melody.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

A world built from **gold keylines on warm black**, filled with **airbrushed hard-edged volumes** (Cassandre, Lempicka), organised around **one vertical axis**. Ornament *is* the picture: sunbursts are backgrounds, stepped arches are frames, a dial is a progress bar, a bulb marquee is a reveal. Motion is **mechanical and symmetrical**: things unfold from the centre, doors split along the seam, lights switch on in counted order. Native register: glamour with a clock ticking (an event, a deadline, a launch).

Not a gold-foil slideshow (things move and have volume), not Art Nouveau (no whiplash curves, no flowers), not a flat vector poster (volumes are airbrushed and rimmed), not a 60s spy title (no silhouettes on flat colour).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Ground**: warm lacquer black, never neutral grey-black; a night sky may drift toward a deep emerald near the horizon.
- **Gold is a banded metal gradient** (dark – light – hot – light – dark); animate its `sheen` offset for a light sweep.
- **The signature stroke** (`gline`): a dark engraved underline ~1.6 px wider than the line, the gold gradient line, and a hairline highlight on top. Optional glow and a parallel twin (`double`). Nothing gets a black cartoon outline.
- **Volumes**: hard edge + airbrush (`airbrush`): a directional gradient from shade to light inside the shape, one consistent light direction (upper left by default), a thin gold rim on the lit side.
- **Motifs** (sunburst, stepped arch / ziggurat, fish-scale, chevrons, fan, four-point sparkle, speed lines, clock face, dial) are structural (a background, a frame, a transition), not stickers.
- **Perspective is real**: true one-point (mode-7 floors) and two-point perspective through a pinhole camera, so dolly, tilt and pan change perspective instead of scaling flats.
- **Characters are deco too**: about 7 heads tall, tapered streamline bodies, faceted lacquer planes (Lempicka), almond or arc eyes, a one-stroke nose, airbrush + gold rim. Give each lead one or two silhouette marks readable at a quarter of frame height.

## 3. Colour logic

- Three constants: **warm black ground, gold line and metal, ivory** for paper, gloves, light and type.
- **One saturated accent reserved for the protagonist** (or the one object the story follows). It is the only large saturated area, so the eye finds it in any wide shot. A cooler jewel tone may carry secondary surfaces, never competing in area.
- **The one-colour exception**: any single element can be drawn in its own colour through the same fill + keyline + glow (`color` option) while everything else stays gold.
- Always expand hex to six digits in code (three-digit hex breaks colour mixing).
- Examples of the triad (accent / jewel / metal): burgundy / emerald / gold; coral / sapphire / pale gold; jade / plum / rose gold. Our demo's actual values are in DEMO.md.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Type (OFL)**: Limelight (titles), Poiret One (numbers, sign skeletons, plaques), Josefin Sans (subtitles, labels), Italiana (numerals).
- **Titles are architecture**: a stepped gold title bar over an arch or sunburst, optional badge and wings; drawn on in gold, then a sheen sweep.
- **Subtitle card** (`subtitleCard`): a lacquer bar (~88 % black) with stepped ends like the title bar, double gold keyline, Josefin Sans SemiBold ~40–42 px ivory, an optional small speaker icon per voice. It **unfolds from the centre** like every other title, so titles, subtitles and transitions are one system. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s).
- Numbers carry plot without narration: dials, clock faces, floor medallions, badges.

## 5. Motion quality

- **Characters step on twos (12 fps)**; camera, light, bulbs, gold draw-on and sheen run on ones (24 fps). A stepped camera reads as stutter.
- **Everything unfolds from the centre**: a point → a hairline → bars open symmetrically → text rises → wings and sparkle.
- **Draw-on follows the music**: a gold line grows at the speed of the phrase under it and lands on the hit.
- **Bulbs have an ignition overshoot** (~1.6× flash settling in ~0.18 s) and a relay "chunk"; once a sign is lit, a fast chase may run across it.
- **Mechanical easing**: doors, dials and hands move with firm ease-in-out and a small settle, like machinery; nothing floats.
- **Performance beats get anticipation** and escalation in threes (once, twice, mash).
- What never moves: the centre axis of a composition. Symmetry may rotate or open, but it never drifts off-centre.

## 6. Camera grammar

A vocabulary, not a route. Opening and ending come from the topic.

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Symmetric split (two door leaves hinged at the edges; or a revolving-door wipe) | a threshold crossed | a new place; a new chapter; a reveal behind a façade |
| Leaves sliding shut over the live shot | a door closing on a moment | leaving; a decision made; the end of an era |
| Extreme low-angle Cassandre tilt | scale and aspiration | a goal far above; a tower, a rocket, a monument |
| Architectural section (pull out to a cutaway of the whole building) | progress through a structure | climbing, descending, a process in stages; a company's floors |
| Busby Berkeley overhead, mirrored and rotating | people become pattern | a team, a release, a celebration, a system of parts |
| Push-in on a dial, medallion or clock | the number is the plot | a deadline; a count; a milestone |
| Match-cut on shape (circle → circle, ray → ray) | two places, one rhyme | jumping between departments, cities, eras |
| Low oblique along a sign or marquee | light travelling letter by letter | a name revealed; a launch; a score being counted |
| Pull back from detail to skyline | where the moment sits in the world | aftermath; a city-wide effect; scale |

Framing: the centre axis is sacred; an asymmetric frame must resolve to it within the shot. At an emotional peak the protagonist fills ≥ ~1/3 of frame height (smaller, the face reads as a prop in the ornament). Transitions: splits, revolves, arch openings, shape matches; never a generic dissolve or slide.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Symphonic jazz of the 1920s–30s, not a 60s big band.** Options: stride or concert piano, clarinet (trill; a glissando by time-varying resampling of a long note), strings (tremolo, rushes, pizzicato), muted trumpet commentary, trombone and sax section, walking pizz bass, brushes or sticks, tubular bells, harp glissandi, banjo, xylophone runs, celesta.
- Rhythm families to choose from: foxtrot, Charleston, tango, a slow torch-song ballad, a fanfare in the manner of a newsreel.
- **Techniques (options)**: one hit per unit of counted light; accelerate by dividing the beat; plant a theme in fragments so its full statement is a payoff; low-pass a band that is physically far away and open it as we approach; move a period narrator through acoustic spaces (horn, radio, PA, live mic) to make distance audible.
- **Foley by material**: brass clicks, bronze clang + chain, iron treads, marble heels, silver trays, wooden doors + spring twang, paper flutter, knife-switch "chunk" + filament hum, relay ticks, elevator ding, champagne cork.
- **Silence as a tool**: before the most important sound, drop to one small diegetic sound (a clock tick, wind) and cut back in with that sound alone.
- **J/L-cuts** carry architecture: the next room's sound enters a bar before its door opens.
- Mix: duck music ~−9 dB under voice (less under a period announcer who is part of the texture), beds −6 dB, −14 LUFS, light film grain.

## 8. Native moves

A menu: use the ones your story needs.

- **Counted light.** A bulb sign lights one letter per beat or per event, so the audience can count. *Fits content like:* the countdown to a product launch; the letters of a city name lighting as a train arrives; votes tallied into a winner.
- **Threshold doors.** Every scene change is a door split along the seam. *Fits content like:* the departments of a company; the rooms of a museum; stages of a career.
- **Machine kaleidoscope.** People or objects become a mirrored, rotating pattern that locks into a symbol. *Fits content like:* a team becoming a logo; gears of a supply chain; a choir becoming a clock.
- **Dials carry the plot.** A floor indicator, a clock or a gauge moves instead of narration. *Fits content like:* a funding thermometer; the altitude of a climb; a stock ticker at the opening bell.
- **The architectural cutaway.** Pull out until a building is a section and the protagonist a coloured dot with speed lines. *Fits content like:* data moving through a server stack; a letter through a post office; a skier down a resort.
- **Sheen sweep / draw-on.** Light crosses a gold object on a hit; a gold line engraves itself at the speed of a glissando. *Fits content like:* unveiling a trophy; a map route; a signature on a treaty.
- **The one colour.** One element keeps its own colour in a gold world. *Fits content like:* the one product among competitors; the patient among doctors; the new idea in an old firm.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- Bulb signs from glyph skeletons break on curves (G, S, R): Zhang–Suen staircase pixels fool a neighbour-count junction test → use the **crossing number** and weld chain ends within ~14 px.
- A generic cartoon character looks pasted in → characters are deco (§2).
- Fish-scale reads as brickwork → lower half-circles row by row, each overlapping the previous row, plus an inner arc.
- Door leaves over a flat "interior" read as a blank frame → draw only the leaves, closing over the live shot.
- A gold point on pure black trips `blackdetect` → lift the background wedges and glow slightly.
- Period loudspeaker distortion is unintelligible under music → gentle drive; whisper-check every line on the final mix.

## 10. Engine

Canvas2D, deterministic in `t`, in `demo/engine/`: `deco.js` (gold gradient, `gline`, `airbrush`, motifs, `drawShape` for any path in the deco manner, `color` for the one-colour exception), `type.js` (title bar, digits, badges, dial, clock, `subtitleCard`), `bulbs.js` (any text → bulb sign, `litSequence`), `cam.js` (pinhole camera, `cardTransform`). `demo/frames.js` renders model sheets and style frames from the real engine. Signatures and a minimal example that draws something not in the demo: DEMO.md "Engine reference".

## 11. Variation space

You decide the structure, the characters (or none), the settings, the opening, the ending, the camera path, the pacing, the accent colour and what gets counted. All far from our demo:

- Structures: **the exhibition** (five pavilions of a world's fair, one idea of the topic behind each door); **the ocean liner** (three decks from engine room to ballroom, a horn per stage); **the trophy night** (nominees as sunburst panels, the winner revealed in light).
- Openings: **the machine room** (gold gears and pistons building to the first beat); **the engraved map** (a gold route crosses a continent before anyone appears); **the telegram** (ticker tape types the premise).
- Endings: **the lights go out** (letters switch off in reverse until one bulb remains); **the dawn** (lacquer black warms to a pale sky); **the poster** (the last shot flattens into a printed poster with a date).

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.
