# Brick Toy — our demo

One example among many. Don't reuse its story, arc, shots, props or timings.

Demo: *Rocket from Spare Parts* (54 s) · `brick-toy.mp4` · source in [`demo/`](demo/) · asset credits [`demo/CREDITS`](demo/CREDITS)

## Story & structure

A brick astronaut builds a rocket; it collapses; he rebuilds it from the fallen parts and flies to the "moon" (a stack of books). Failure isn't the end, it's just spare parts. One character, one goal.

The old guide told agents to "turn the topic into something being built" and to use at least three of the four native powers; the demo used all four: snap-together building (open on one brick, end on one brick), break without harm (the collapse becomes the parts for a better rocket), toy on a real desk (a teapot is a mountain, a stack of books is the moon, the lamp is the sun), hand-made stop-motion (12 fps, even the flames and smoke are bricks). The old guide also listed adaptation examples: a product launch → the product is assembled brick by brick; a love story → two characters build a bridge between two books; a history lesson → an era is built, falls, is rebuilt.

Arc (45–60 s, as written for this film): curiosity → excitement → a setback (collapse) → a quiet beat → rebuilding → climax → a warm scale-reveal. Acts: opening 0:00–0:06 (one red brick, the first snap), act one 0:06–0:18 (fast building, pride), act two 0:18–0:30 (collapse, silence, picking up the parts), act three 0:30–0:50 (countdown, ignition, launch, landing on the moon), end card after.

## Shots

| Beat | Camera |
|---|---|
| Opening | Extreme macro on one brick, slow push, background blurred to real props |
| Building | Low angles make the tiny character heroic; cut every bar |
| Setback | Handheld shake on the collapse, then a **low, wide, lonely** frame with the character small |
| Emotional beat | Close-up from the front, character's hands and the brick in focus |
| Climax | Low angle following upward; then a **tracking shot** alongside the rocket with the moon (books) visible ahead |
| Ending | Slow pull-back to a high wide shot of the whole desk: the scale reveal |

Each of these is one choice from STYLE.md §6 made for this story, not the style's default opening or ending.

Lens settings as used: aperture ~500–700 for close-ups, ~800 for mediums, ~400 for the final wide. Snap overshoot 0.35 stud → 0 in ~0.17 s. Collapse gravity ~420 studs/s² (true would be 1225), restitution ~0.3.

## Score structure

Two Kevin MacLeod tracks (CC BY 4.0), edited to the picture by `demo/music/edit.py`: "Monkeys Spinning Monkeys" (playful, cut on bars) for building, the same theme returning quietly for the rebuild, "Heroic Age" as the orchestral swell for the climax. The edit makes the climax hit land on ignition and the final chord land on the end card (bar-aligned jumps, chroma similarity at the joins). `story.js` times are aligned to the music bars.

Silences: music cut dead on the collapse, leaving room tone and a ticking clock; music pulled out again before the climax, with a low heartbeat drum under the countdown.

Foley specific to this film: ignition boom and rocket roar; radio chatter with Quindar beeps.

Voice: warm British storyteller, Kokoro `bm_george`, speed ~0.9, 4–6 short lines; mission control is `am_adam` through a radio filter (band-pass 380–2800 Hz + soft saturation) with Quindar beeps. Every line verified with whisper. Voice compressed, music ducked ~40 % under voice, −14 LUFS.

## Palette & props

- Classic brick palette: red `#c91a09`, blue `#0055bf`, yellow `#f2cd37`, green `#237841`, white `#f2f2ee`, black `#1b2a34`, plus orange, light/dark grey, tan, azure. Bevel radius 0.06; baseplate matte green (it turned cyan with full clearcoat).
- Set: walnut desk (Poly Haven `american_walnut_veneer`), `photo_studio_loft_hall` HDRI, tea set (teapot mountain, cup), pencil, books (the moon), desk lamp (the sun). Key light `#fff4e8` from upper left; softboxes key front-left, cool rim behind, one over the finale set. GTAO radius ~3.5 studs, scale 2.5. Grade: contrast +0.26, saturation ×1.1, slightly cool.
- The astronaut: 1×1 columns for legs, a 2×2 brick torso, round-brick arms, a round 2×2 helmet with a curved visor panel.
- The rocket, fire (translucent orange/yellow round plates jittered every frame), smoke (white round bricks that grow and roll outward), the moon (grey round plates with crater tiles).
- Subtitles: a dark rounded pill `rgba(18,20,26,.62)` centred 150 px above the bottom, Fredoka 600 46 px white, a small yellow 2×1 brick icon on the left. Radio lines get a red brick icon and a "MISSION CONTROL" tag.
- Title: "Rocket from Spare Parts", Fredoka 700, popping in on 12 fps steps, with the yellow sub-line "A BRICK TOY FILM".

## End card

The darkened final wide, the title (Fredoka 700), a brick icon, "BRICK TOY · LEMO-OPUSCAR" in yellow, the "LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5" line and the asset credits. That sign-off belongs to this library's demo only; a user's film carries no LemoLab credit and no copy of this card (remove the line drawn in `main.js` if you adapt it).

## Build notes

```
styles/brick-toy/demo/
  bricks.js   geometry + plastic materials        rockets.js  props, physics, fx
  actors.js   brick-built character rig            set.js      desk, HDRI, real props, moon
  story.js    timeline aligned to music bars        main.js     acting, cameras, subtitles, events
  lines.json  voice script    mix.py  foley+voice+music    music/edit.py  score edit
```

1. `node core/render/still.mjs styles/brick-toy/demo <t…>`: review stills, iterate.
2. `.venv/bin/python core/tts/tts.py lines.json voices` → `core/tts/asr_check.py` to verify.
3. `node core/render/events.mjs styles/brick-toy/demo` → `python music/edit.py` → `python mix.py`.
4. `node core/render/video.mjs styles/brick-toy/demo --fps 24` (1296 frames with 2× SSAA + GTAO ≈ 65 s on an M4 Pro).
5. `core/render/mux.sh out/video24.mp4 mix.wav brick-toy.mp4 24`.

Pitfalls tied to this demo's props:
- The helmet visor made from a sphere segment disappeared inside the cylinder helmet; a curved open-cylinder panel fixed it.
- The rocket simply accelerating upward became a dot on a blank wall; a tracking shot aimed at the moon fixed it.
- The desk lamp, placed on the camera axis of a later shot, kept sneaking into the background.
- Stepping the camera at 12 fps too was tried and looked unsmooth; the camera moved to ones.
- Spare-parts piles kept blocking the lens at frame edges.

# Brick Toy — Style Prompt

> Stop-motion toy-brick films shot like macro photography on a real desk: a world built from interlocking plastic bricks with round studs, animated a pose at a time.
> References (grammar only): brick-film stop-motion on a tabletop and the "brick movie" approach of stepping characters while the camera moves smoothly; macro toy photography (softboxes on glossy plastic, shallow focus, real objects as landscape). Copy none of their characters, sets or music, and never use a brand name.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

A brick world on a **real surface** (a wooden desk, a kitchen table, a windowsill), shot with a **macro lens** and animated **in stop-motion**. The charm is the tension between the toy world and the real room.

One-glance traits: glossy ABS with clean rectangular highlights; studs on every top face; seams darkened by contact shadow; real objects out of focus behind; characters that move in held poses on twos.

**Never** use the LEGO name, logo or minifigure silhouette (trademarks). Characters are *built from bricks* (e.g. 1×1 columns for legs, a 2×2 brick for a torso, round bricks for arms, a round 2×2 helmet). Studs carry no lettering.

Not a low-poly isometric island (no flat-shaded facets, no floating diorama), not a clay or felt stop-motion (no deformation: bricks are rigid), not a clean product render of a toy (this world is played with, handled, knocked over).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Plastic**: ABS with strong clearcoat (~0.85, clearcoat roughness ~0.07); a roughness map with faint fingerprints and scratches (base ~0.17, scratches up to ~0.65); a bevel so edges catch a highlight.
- **Geometry**: rounded box bodies (bevel ~0.045 stud), studs with a thin lip. Unit = 1 stud pitch (8 mm); brick height 1.2, plate 0.4. Large baseplates are **matte** (lower clearcoat than bricks), or they reflect softboxes as a coloured wash.
- **Set**: a real surface with a real texture and real props at true scale (1 m = 125 studs). Household objects become landscape. Light it with a **neutral daylight studio HDRI**, never a tungsten interior (white bricks turn orange).
- **Light**: a toy-photography setup. A directional key from one upper side, warm-white, casting shadows (fit its shadow frustum to each shot so shadows stay crisp); two or three **RectAreaLight softboxes** (key front, cool rim behind, one over any big set) so glossy plastic shows clean rectangular highlights; environment kept low (~0.45) for contrast. Add a soft contact-shadow blob where the key's shadow falls behind a hero object.
- **Ambient occlusion is mandatory**: GTAO (radius a few studs) darkens seams between stacked bricks, stud bases and contact points. Without it bricks look pasted on.
- **Supersample 2×** (render 3840×2160, deliver 1080p): thin stud edges and bevel highlights shimmer without it.
- **Lens**: physical depth of field (CoC ∝ |1/focus − 1/z|). Scale aperture with shot size: widest for close-ups, less for mediums, least for a wide (too much blurs the hero at mid distance). Focus is always on a character's head or the brick being placed.
- **Effects are bricks**: fire, smoke, water, light, weather, celestial bodies are all built from plates, round bricks and translucent pieces, jittered or rebuilt per drawing. Nothing is a particle system or a soft gradient.

## 3. Colour logic

- A **toy palette**: a handful of saturated brick primaries plus white, black, greys, tan. Each built object has one dominant colour and at most one or two trim colours; characters and hero objects take the most saturated ones.
- The **real world stays natural and muted**: wood, paper, ceramic, daylight. The saturated colour belongs to the toys, which makes them pop against the room.
- **Whites must read white**: grade slightly cool so white bricks don't go cream from the room bounce; soft contrast, saturation lifted ~10 %.
- Translucent pieces (orange, yellow, clear, blue) are reserved for effects: fire, light, water, glass.
- Example palette (the classic brick primaries): red `#c91a09`, blue `#0055bf`, yellow `#f2cd37`, green `#237841`, white `#f2f2ee`, black `#1b2a34`. Others: pastels and tan; greys with one accent.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- A rounded, friendly OFL face (e.g. Fredoka, in `core/fonts`) for titles and subtitles.
- Subtitles live on a **toy element**: a dark rounded pill low in the frame with a small brick icon beside the text, or a printed tile, or a sign built into the set. White on dark, ≤ 2 lines. A second speaker type (radio, device, narrator) gets its own icon colour or tag. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s).
- Titles pop in on 12 fps steps, like a piece being placed; a short sub-line in a brick colour.

## 5. Motion quality

- **Characters and bricks step at 12 fps** (on twos); **camera, focus, fire and flying vehicles move on ones** at 24 fps. Stepping the camera too reads as judder, not charm.
- Bricks **fly in on arcs** and **snap** with a tiny overshoot (a fraction of a stud → 0 in ~4 frames). Every snap is a click on the soundtrack.
- Characters act with **big readable poses** held for several drawings: a V of arms for pride, arms flung up for alarm, a bowed head for sadness, a hop for joy. Walk cycles swing legs about ±0.55 rad with a small bob. Arms and legs rotate at their joints; nothing bends.
- Collapses and falls use **real rigid-body physics**: tip about the base edge, then independent bodies with gravity (a lower-than-true value reads better at this scale), bounces (restitution ~0.3), friction, settling flat. Pre-simulate so every render is identical.
- Tiny imperfections are allowed. Bricks never stretch, squash or morph.

## 6. Camera grammar

A vocabulary, not a route. Opening and ending come from the topic.

| Move | Expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Extreme macro on one brick or stud, real room blurred behind | The toy scale is the world | a beginning; a detail that matters; a single part |
| Low angle at minifig eye level | A tiny character made heroic | ambition; pride; standing up to something big |
| High wide over the whole surface | The scale reveal: it was a toy all along | a summing-up; irony; a finished build |
| Low, wide, lonely frame, character small in a corner | Smallness, failure | a setback; waiting; loss |
| Frontal close-up, hands and brick in focus | Intimacy, decision | a choice; a repair; a gift |
| Handheld shake on impact | Physical shock | a collapse; an arrival; a collision |
| Tracking alongside a moving object, destination ahead | Momentum toward a goal | a journey; a race; a launch |
| Top-down plan view | Order, layout, a map | a plan; sorting parts; a city from above |
| Rack focus from a real object to a brick (or back) | Two scales in one frame | "big world, small maker"; a comparison |
| Orbit around a finished build | Pride, inspection | a product; a monument; a result |

Framing: keep foreground clutter out of the frame edges (piles of parts love to block the lens); check headroom in every shot; check every real prop against every camera, because an object placed on one shot's axis sneaks into the background of another. Cut on beats or bars; a snap can be a cut point. No generic dissolves; transitions can be a hand-placed brick covering the lens, a whip along the desk, or a pull out of one set into the next.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Instruments**: small, acoustic, playful (glockenspiel, toy piano, pizzicato, ukulele, whistling, claps, melodica); a brass or orchestral swell for scale; a heartbeat drum for suspense. Licensed or original, edited to the picture (cut on bars, bar-aligned jumps, chroma similarity at joins) rather than looped under it.
- **Foley** (synthesizable): plastic creak before a failure, tiny plastic footsteps, a crash of many clacks, a brick click (short transient + resonances near 2.9 kHz and 4.6 kHz), clack on wood, rattle of a parts pile being stirred, whoosh on throws, a bell "ding" for discovery, bricks sliding over paper, motors and engines built from filtered noise.
- **Silence is a tool**: cut music dead at a failure or a surprise; leave only room tone and one small real-world sound (a ticking clock, a fridge hum, a distant bird). Music can also drop out before a big moment, leaving a pulse or a countdown.
- **Voice**: a warm storyteller, few short lines with room to breathe; secondary voices through a device filter (band-pass ~380–2800 Hz + soft saturation), optionally with beeps. Verify every line with whisper.
- Mix: voice compressed, music ducked ~40 % under voice, loudness −14 LUFS.

## 8. Native moves

A menu: use the ones your story needs.

- **Snap-together building.** The plot is an act of building; pieces fly in on arcs and click home. *Fits content like:* a company assembling its first product; a neighbourhood rising street by street; a recipe put together ingredient by ingredient.
- **Break without harm.** Things fall apart and the parts become something new; failure yields spare parts. *Fits content like:* a pivot after a failed plan; recycling; a team reshuffled into a better shape.
- **Toy on a real desk.** Real objects become landscape at toy scale. *Fits content like:* a laptop keyboard as a city grid; a houseplant as a jungle; a coffee spill as a flood.
- **Hand-made stop-motion.** 12 fps poses, tiny imperfections, even fire and water made of bricks. *Fits content like:* a weather report; a kitchen explained with brick flames; a science demo of a volcano.
- **Rebuild into something else.** The same pieces, rearranged on screen, become a different object. *Fits content like:* one career turning into another; a before/after renovation; a word re-spelled.
- **The scale reveal.** Pull back until the whole world is a toy on a table. *Fits content like:* a big ambition that is still small; a year in review; a child's imagination.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- Tungsten HDRI → orange whites. Use a neutral studio HDRI and a slightly cool grade.
- Clearcoat on a large flat baseplate reflects softboxes as a coloured wash. Make it matte.
- Flat, slightly jagged first renders: even light, no AO, single-sample rendering, stepped camera. Fix: softboxes + low environment, GTAO, 2× supersampling, cool grade, camera on ones.
- Too much aperture blurs the hero at mid distance. Scale aperture with shot size.
- A fast-rising or fast-moving object becomes a dot on a blank wall. Track it and keep its destination in frame.
- Curved transparent parts made from a sphere segment vanish inside a cylindrical part. Use an open-cylinder panel.
- Real props on a later shot's camera axis sneak into the background. Check props against every camera.
- Random jitter used as a material or colour index can go negative → undefined material crash. Clamp.

## 10. Engine

In `demo/`: `bricks.js` (rounded brick/plate/round-brick geometry, studs, plastic materials with clearcoat and fingerprint roughness), `actors.js` (a brick-built character rig with pose objects and `walkPose`), `set.js` (desk, HDRI, real props at true scale, softboxes), `rockets.js` (props, pre-simulated rigid-body physics, brick fire and smoke), `main.js` (acting, cameras, DOF, subtitles, sound events), `mix.py` (synthesized foley + voice + music), `music/edit.py` (bar-aligned score edit). Minimal start: a brick lighthouse from `bricks.js` on a stack of books, lit by the `set.js` softboxes, one still via `core/render/still.mjs`.

## 11. Variation space

You decide the structure, the characters (or none), the surface and its props, the opening, the ending, the camera path, the pacing, the palette within the colour logic and the music. All far from our demo:

- Structures: **a catalogue** (one build per beat, each a different object answering the same question, lined up at the end); **two builders** on opposite sides of the table whose builds grow toward each other; **a disassembly** (a finished thing is taken apart piece by piece to explain what's inside).
- Openings: **a hand pours a bin of bricks** onto the table and the pile settles into the first shape; **a real object first** (a mug, a phone), then rack focus to the tiny world at its base; **plan view** of an empty baseplate filling in like a map.
- Endings: **one piece left over** held in close-up, the question it raises unanswered; **the lights go out** in the room and only a lit brick window glows; **a real hand** reaches in and picks the character up.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

# Engineering Briefing Board — our demo

One example among many. Don't reuse its story, arc, shots, props or timings.

Demo: *The Ship Decides* (船说了算, 40.0 s) · `briefing-board.mp4` · source in [`demo/`](demo/)

A river 1,000 m wide needs a bridge. The first instinct, piers all the way across, is stamped out the moment a container ship sails into one of them. The new rule: no piers in the channel, one span. Four bridge types are tested against the river's width, drawn to one scale. The river set the question; the ship sets the span.

## Story & structure

Shape: an elimination that turns early. Hook (0–1 s): the river's width snaps across in the first quarter-second. Setup (1–8 s): "1,000 米", a pier-by-pier beam crossing. Turn (8 s): after a second of near-silence the ship touches the centre pier and a red stamp lands. Development (11–27 s): the rule is written, the piers pop off, a steel ruler is laid bank to bank; dashed projection lines carry the banks down into an elevation "test bench" where four photographed bridges land one after another, each met close by the camera as it lands, then judged in a held frame that shows the whole bridge, the two bank lines (the 1,000 m "door"), its dimension line drawn to its record main span, and the verdict landing after the camera has settled. Each judgement frame is wider than the last, so the widening is the rhythm: the cable-stayed line crawls just past the far bank, the suspension line rockets past it and throws the camera. Ending (32.8–40 s): down at the waterline a side-view container ship comes out from behind the far tower and sails under the suspension span; half a second of room tone; then the only pull-back, starting from the ship, to the whole wall, where the verdict "船决定跨度" is written beside the results. The final frame is the poster.

Why it fits the style: one continuous wall holds a plan view (top-down ship, river, crossing) above an elevation view (side-on bridges) with projection lines between them — a real drafting convention, so a top-down ship and side-on bridges share one board without breaking geometry. The same ship appears in both views: the problem in plan, the answer in elevation. Native moves spent: magnets as countable things, the stamp, erase to a ghost, the physical answer (the ruler), projection lines, ride the dimension line (four times), the subject passes through the answer, leader to the verdict, and the whole-wall reveal as the signature shot.

## Shots

One continuous camera, no cuts. Times in seconds; zoom 1 = 1,920 board px across.

| 2 | 1.2–2.9 | MCU on "1,000 米" being written | push in (z 1.42), roll +1° | |

## Score structure

- 120 BPM, 4/4, D minor → D major at the reveal. Instruments: electric bass (eighth-note figure), MuldjordKit kick/snare/hats, claves, shaker, low brass stabs (trombone, tuba, horn), timpani, gran cassa, crash, tubular bells, glockenspiel, vibraphone. No piano, no string pad.
- Arc: the hook (Dm brass stab, low tom, kick with the snapping line at 0.25) → groove A → low-pass dive → **silence 7.0–8.0** → stamp: Dm brass stab + timpani + gran cassa → half time (held D, low toms) → groove A rebuilt under the rule → groove B (kit) under the test bench, one brass stab per landing in the bar's chord, a sour trombone blat (D + E♭) per strike → the cable crawl: bass climbs chromatically in eighths G1 → G2 with a shaker swell → "just enough": two horn notes → snare sixteenths into the suspension's line (A, dominant, on the landing) → the line lands: crash + a bright B♭ chord (VI) → vibraphone pair on the ring → bass whole notes and soft trombone fifths under the last line and the ship → **silence 35.25–35.75** → the reveal: the ship's horn tuned to D (root and fifth) with a D-major brass chord, timpani and tubular bells → the verdict is written to a horn line A–F♯–E–D–A → glockenspiel D–F♯–A–D while the wall settles.
- Hits: every landing, pin, stamp, arrow, strike and tag sits on the 16th-note grid (`tools/cuecheck.py`: 27/27 at 0 ms).
- Foley (procedural, `audio/mix.py`): felt-tip squeaks scaled to stroke length, nib taps, magnet clacks pitched per pier, two pin clacks after every landing, suction pops, print landings (board thump + paper slap, heavier for the suspension), the steel ruler's ring, eraser felt, rubber stamp, ship horn (far and near), diesel rumble, water lapping, whooshes, room tone with distant traffic.
- J-cuts: the horn at 5.75 before the top-down ship is seen; the horn at 32.0 before the side-view ship comes out from behind the tower. L-cuts: the eraser over the move into the bench; the reveal horn over the whole pull-back.
- Mix: music about 9 dB under the voice and ducked; foley ducked under speech; room tone (air conditioning on the right, traffic through the window on the left) about 20 dB under the voice and never ducked; silences gated to that room tone; −14 LUFS integrated.
- Voice: Kokoro `af_heart`, nine lines; numbers spelled out for TTS and written as digits in the subtitles.

## Palette & props

- Board 6,400 × 3,600 board px (16:9, so the final pull-back fills the frame); enamel `#F3F1EB`; wall `#8F8B83`; ink graphite `#23272E`, blue `#1F4FC8`, red `#D33A21`, water hatching `#5F86DA`, drafting grey `#6C727B`.
- Plan view (top left): river 1,240 px = 1,000 m between two blue banks with grey ground hatching; "1,000 米" above; crossing with seven graphite magnets; the top-down ship scaled to 500 px (about true scale); stamp "否决" (Noto Sans SC 900, pitted red). Rule "新规矩" red with an underline, "航道不立墩" graphite (LXGW Marker Gothic). The ruler: brushed steel with engraved graduations, a magnet at each end.
- Elevation (left two-thirds): projection lines dashed blue; four rows scaled so each main span is its record length at 1.24 px per metre (330, 600, 1,208, 2,023 m); each print pinned by two magnets; under each arrow end a label block: a name tag (Noto Sans SC 700, 78 px) and the number in blue marker (100 px), the tag placed by the number's measured width so they never touch. The side-view ship is 340 px long (about true scale) on a hand-drawn waterline. The cable-stayed bridge is a mirrored composite of a single-pylon photo and the suspension bridge's main span is stretched ×1.7 (see `demo/CREDITS`).
- Right third (never in shot before the reveal): four photo prints with magnets (suspension, cable-stayed, arch, and the side-view ship whose lettering was wiped), a source card ("数据来源"), two sticky notes with the sums (1,208 − 1,000 = 208; 2,023 ÷ 1,000 ≈ 2), a small navigation-clearance sketch without numbers, the verdict "船决定跨度" (400 px, "船" red) at the right middle with a leader from the circled 2,023, and the end card.
- Subtitles: frosted strip, Chinese Noto Sans SC 500 42 px over English Archivo 500 29 px, blue tick at left; every cue measured on one line per language (`tools/subcheck.mjs`).

## Title card

A printed card pinned at the bottom right of the wall from the start, seen only in the reveal: "船说了算", a red rule, "ENGINEERING / BRIEFING BOARD", "工程简报板", "LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5". It is part of the final wall (the poster) and is on screen for the last three seconds. The "LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5" sign-off belongs to this library's demo only; a user's film carries no LemoLab credit and no copy of this card.

  audio/lines.json      narration (Kokoro)          audio/mix.py   score, foley, voice, mix

1. `sh demo/build.sh` (library set up with `setup.sh deps voice music`): fetches what git does not hold — fonts from Google Fonts (`fetch_fonts.py`: Archivo and IBM Plex Mono from github.com/google/fonts, the CJK subsets through the CSS API), the six photos from Commons (`fetch_sources.py`, ~470 MB), a private `demo/.venv` with onnxruntime and the BiRefNet model (`kit_env.sh`, ~970 MB unless cached), the voice model and the freepats / vsco2ce / vcsl samples — and cuts the objects again (`rebuild_objects.sh`); then speech check → scene → cue check → reading check → camera check (incl. judgement frames) → resolution check → events → render (960 frames, 5 workers) → mix → subtitles (+ one-line check) → mux (−14 LUFS, grain 1) → poster and styleframe → rhythm report → speech check on the final mix → camera plot.
2. Objects: `sh demo/kit/tools/rebuild_objects.sh` recreates every cut-out from the photos at their own resolution (BiRefNet masks are cached in `sources/masks/`; a recomputed mask can differ by a pixel or two from ours).
3. Stills and thumbnails: a scene JSON that `extends` `scenes/film.json` with its own `cam` and `t`, rendered by `node demo/kit/batch.mjs`.

Bridge-specific choices: each landing is met close on a pylon top, an arch rib, the hangers or a pier's foot; stays, main cables and hangers are redrawn as clean lines at the positions measured in the photos. Pitfalls tied to this demo: the first cut rode each dimension line close and never showed the cable-stayed or suspension bridge whole; viewers lost what was being tested ("too fast"). The fix was the judgement frame per bridge, held, widening each time, with the voice and the verdict inside the hold. Text first glimpsed during a move failed the reading check, so every label block is pinned where the camera rests and each new row is framed with the previous row's result. The first cut-outs were downscaled and the close-ups upsampled them (a blocky ship); every object is now cut at full resolution and `rescheck.mjs` caps each zoom. Keyed stays turned into stair-steps and arch hangers vanished against the hills; stays and suspension cables are now measured and redrawn, the arch hangers continued to the deck. Name tags at a fixed offset overlapped the wider numbers; they are placed from the number's measured advance width. The stretched suspension photo allows z 1.38 at most, so its landing close-up is on the near tower, which is not stretched. The photographed suspension bridge has the proportions of a 500 m span; scaled uniformly to 2,023 m its towers would be far too tall, so only the main span is stretched. A road sign, a water-level gauge, a ship's name and container logos were removed (lettering). The pier clacks masked "piers" in the voice; they were lowered.

# Engineering Briefing Board — Style Prompt

> One real whiteboard wall, filmed: window light on enamel, ghosts of erased marker, frame and tray. Cut-out photographs of real things land on it with weight; tags, magnets, a ruler and stamps are pinned to it; marker ink draws itself in three colours with fixed meanings. The camera rides the lines from fact to fact and only at the end pulls back to show the whole briefing.
> References (grammar only): explainers filmed on a map wall; the long pull-back over a wall covered in work; drafting conventions (plan above elevation, dimension lines, hatching). Never copy them or name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

1. **A physical board in a room**: enamel, window falloff, a sliding reflection, ghosts of earlier work, frame and tray.
2. **Real things on it**: cut-out photographs of the real objects, a few millimetres off the board, shadowed by one window, parallaxing. They are evidence: never a generated image presented as a real object.
3. **Ink that means something**: graphite for names and rules, blue for water and measurement, red only for the decision; rejected ideas erased to ghosts.
4. **One continuous wall**: no pages; the camera travels along lines, projections and leaders.
5. **The whole wall, once**: every shot is a crop of the final briefing, seen whole only in the last pull-back, as a poster.

Not **Whiteboard Explainer** (a hand drawing line art on a flat page): the board is a filmed object, subjects are photographs. Not **Data Storytelling**: comparisons are dimension lines in real units beside real objects. Not a keynote: no headers, centred bullets, page turns.

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Board (z 0)**: procedural enamel, wiped ghost strokes, smudges, a window falloff, a sliding diagonal reflection; the frame shadows a warm grey wall.
- **Ink (multiply)**: flat colour at about 90 %, lighter core, round caps, a wet-tip glint on the stroke being drawn. Lettering: a marker font revealed glyph by glyph with seeded tilt and baseline jitter. Erasing leaves a blurred ghost (about 7 %).
- **Prints (z ≈ 6–14)**: photographs cut out at full resolution (a matting model, or a hand polygon / mask), clean edges, one shared grade (lower saturation, a touch warmer, lifted blacks). Thin structure (cables, wires, masts, railings) is measured in the photo and redrawn as clean lines in one colour. Shadow = blurred silhouette along one light vector, softer the higher the object. **No frame upsamples a photo**: ≥ 1 source px per screen px at its largest, measured; cap the zoom or find a bigger source.
- **Secondary layer** (only where the camera never goes before the end): the photos as pinned prints, a source card, sums on sticky notes, a small sketch. Texture and proof for the final wall, lighter than the main line.
- **Props (z ≈ 8–26)**: magnetic tags, magnets, a steel ruler, printed cards, a pitted stamp impression; the tray (z 70) nearest the lens.
- **Camera**: parallax by height, sub-frame motion blur (180° shutter), light grain. Only subtitles are screen-space.

## 3. Colour logic

- Ground: the enamel and its light falloff; the wall around is neutral warm grey.
- Ink: graphite = names, rules, facts; blue = water and measurement (dimensions, projection lines, measured numbers); red = the decision (a rejection, the key word of a verdict, the one mark to notice); grey for drafting only (extension lines, hatching).
- Red is rare: two or three red marks per frame at most, never on a red object. Full colour belongs to the photographs; props stay neutral; a red magnet is a verdict.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **Marker lettering**: a single-weight marker face covering every script the film uses (ours: LXGW Marker Gothic, OFL, subset — re-run when words change). Content 100–160 board px; a verdict 230–400.
- **Printed labels** (tags, cards, stamps): a sturdy sans; credit lines in a monospace. A tag holds one to three words.
- **Subtitles**: a frosted acrylic strip at the bottom centre with a blue marker tick. If the film is bilingual, the film's language sits on top. **One line per language**: `nowrap`, measured in the page against a 1,500 px safe width; a long line becomes two cues. Key content stays above the strip (bottom 15 %).
- **Reading time**: subtitles ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s); board text stays fully in frame for CJK ÷ 4.5 + other ÷ 15 + 1.5 s from when it appears. In the final wall, text meant to be read is ≥ 20 px on screen.

## 5. Motion quality

- 24 fps on ones; nothing is stepped.
- Camera: overlapping eased moves, velocity ∝ u^a (1−u)^b (a, b ≈ 1.5–4), so speed and acceleration never jump; b > a gives inertia. A hand-held breath (≤ 3 px) underneath; shake only on an impact.
- Weight: prints are lowered from the camera side, land, bounce and settle as the shadow tightens; magnets clack on to pin them; tags swing; removed magnets pop toward the lens; struck things jolt and spring back. The camera may meet a landing close, briefly, on the object's most telling detail, then pulls out.
- Blurred in motion, sharp where words are read. Every 1–2 beats something lands, draws or swings; only silences and judgement holds go still.
- Ink draws at the speed of a hand; dimension lines land with an arrowhead tap.
- Never: dissolves, scale-pops on text, bouncy UI easing, text fading in by itself.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Ride a line (with the pen or a dimension) | measuring; "how far does it go?" | lengths compared; a route; a timeline |
| Tilt along projection lines | the same quantity in another view | plan → elevation; a total → its parts |
| Slow push-in, slight Dutch tilt | tension, an approaching problem | a collision; a deadline; an overrun |
| Pull back and sideways | stepping back to state a rule | a constraint; a turn in the argument |
| Whip with the line, overshoot, settle | a result that exceeds | a record; an outlier |
| Rise along a leader line | from evidence to verdict | a conclusion; a recommendation |
| Staircase framing (each new item with the previous result) | comparison in sequence | rankings; tests; options |
| Judgement frame: the whole item, the limit and the verdict, held ≥ 2.5 s | a test the viewer can check | pass / fail against a threshold; a budget against a cap |
| Long pull-back to the whole wall | scale; everything at once | the end of an argument; a summary |

Framing: off-centre, cropped, close. The first frame holds a readable subject; the first strong action hits within 0.5 s. Items tested against a limit each get a judgement frame (wider each time if they grow); the verdict lands after the camera settles. Before the reveal: ≤ about 60 % of the board's width, never both side edges, never the reveal's zone. Transitions are moves; no cuts, fades or zoom-to-fit.

## 7. Sound palette

- Room: an air-conditioning bed and traffic through the window, about 20 dB under the voice — audible, not a hiss; silences keep only this.
- Foley: felt-tip squeaks scaled to stroke length, nib taps, magnet clacks (a pitch per magnet in a row), suction pops, print landings (board thump, paper slap), a ruler's ring, eraser felt, a stamp's thud.
- The subject's own sound arrives early as a J-cut; the first sound after a silence is an impact or the subject's sound.
- Music: a small rhythmic ensemble, walking to brisk — bass, a light kit, wooden percussion, low brass stabs for verdicts (or mallets); no piano-and-strings pad. Landings, stamps and arrows sit on the beat. Voice calm, briefing-room confident, about 8–10 dB over the music; −14 LUFS.

## 8. Native moves

- **The whole-wall reveal.** Design the wall as a poster first (hierarchy, reading path, filling the frame), then plan every shot as a crop of it; keep one zone (secondary layer, verdict, title card) for the reveal alone. *Fits:* a product roadmap; a household budget.
- **The subject passes through the answer.** The real thing moves through the chosen solution, its sound first. *Fits:* a parcel along the chosen route; a train over the new viaduct.
- **Ride the dimension line.** A quantity drawn as a real length to one scale; the camera rides the tip. *Fits:* battery ranges of four cars.
- **Projection lines.** Dashed lines carry an edge from one view to another so two drawings share a scale. *Fits:* a trail map above its elevation profile.
- **Magnets as countable things.** Units clack on in rhythm, pop off when a rule removes them. *Fits:* seats in a vote.
- **Erase to a ghost.** A rejected idea wiped but faintly visible. *Fits:* last year's plan under this year's.
- **The stamp.** A verdict lands with a thud and a jolt. *Fits:* passed / failed tests.
- **The physical answer.** A real prop laid down as the solution. *Fits:* one cable instead of five.
- **Leader to the verdict.** An arrow from the deciding number to the conclusion. *Fits:* the bottleneck in a process.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Text glimpsed in passing** fails the reading time. Fix: words where the camera rests; frame each new item with the last result.
- **Only close-ups.** The viewer never sees the whole object against the limit. Fix: detail → judgement frame → hold → verdict → move on.
- **Photos that don't belong together.** Fix: one grade, one light vector, one viewpoint family.
- **Thin parts lost or stair-stepped** by the matte. Fix: key them against the clean background, redraw clean lines at the measured positions.
- **Upsampled photos** go soft in close-ups. Fix: full-resolution cuts, large sources, a per-frame check.
- **Lettering in photos** (signs, names, logos). Fix: paint out, cut, or choose another photo.
- **The wall seen too early** spends the ending; **a sparse or tiny final wall** wastes it. Fix: measure every frame's visible share; size the hierarchy for the poster; a quiet secondary layer, no empty middle.

## 10. Sources, facts, engine

- **Photos**: Wikimedia Commons (read each file page's licence and author), national libraries and archives (e.g. the Library of Congress: check each item's rights statement), agency media pages, Flickr Commons. Fine: CC0, public domain, CC BY (credit it). CC BY-SA, "no known restrictions" (≠ CC0) or other terms: name them to the user and ask first. For the user's own product, site or people, ask for their photos. No licensable photo of a real thing → draw it in marker as a sketch; never a generated image presented as the real object.
- **Facts**: keep a `FACTS.md` in the project folder (each claim on screen or in the voice, its source URL, the quoted wording, or the measurement method) and deliver it with the film. List every photo in `CREDITS` with source, author and licence.
- **Extra packages and packs** (beyond `setup.sh deps voice music`): `onnxruntime` and the BiRefNet-general matting model (MIT, ~970 MB: https://github.com/danielgatis/rembg/releases/download/v0.0.0/BiRefNet-general-epoch_244.onnx, path in `$BIREFNET_ONNX`) for cut-outs; `fonttools` only to subset CJK fonts offline. The agent installs them itself into a private venv in the project folder (`demo/kit/tools/kit_env.sh` does venv and model), never into `$LIB/.venv`. Without the model: cut with `prep_object.py --poly` (hand polygon) or `--mask` (a mask image).
- **Engine** (copy into the project): `demo/kit/board.js` (camera, prints, tags, magnets, ruler, cards, stamp, ink, erasing, `sceneTexts(t)`, `subCheck()`; fields in `demo/kit/README.md`), `demo/kit/batch.mjs` (stills), `demo/kit/tools/` (cut-outs, line redraws, lettering wipe, prints, fonts), checks in `demo/tools/` (`camcheck.mjs` visible share and judgement frames, `rescheck.mjs`, `subcheck.mjs`).

A minimal world (`node demo/kit/batch.mjs park.json`; `fetch_fonts.py park.json` first for new characters):

```json
{ "dur": 6, "t": 5.5, "board": { "w": 4000, "h": 2400 }, "hand": 0, "cam": { "x": 1500, "y": 1000, "z": 0.8, "moves": [] },
  "elements": [
    { "type": "tag", "text": "地下车库", "xy": [560, 800], "size": 60, "arrive": { "t": 0.2, "kind": "swing" } },
    { "type": "ink", "kind": "dim", "from": [700, 900], "to": [1300, 900], "color": "blue", "t": 0.6, "d": 0.6 },
    { "type": "ink", "kind": "write", "text": "120 米", "xy": [1360, 940], "size": 100, "color": "blue", "t": 1.2 },
    { "type": "stamp", "text": "首选", "xy": [1500, 700], "size": 110, "rot": -8, "t": 4.2 } ] }
```

## 11. Variation space

The agent decides per film: structure, which objects are photographed, plan vs elevation, the wall's reading path, opening, ending, camera path, pacing.

- **Three structures:** one measurement that keeps growing until it breaks a limit; a before/after where the erased first plan stays as a ghost under the second; a checklist stamped item by item as the camera moves down the wall.
- **Three openings:** a stamp on a finished drawing, then back to see why; one number written large, then the line that measures it; a photo dropped onto an empty corner.
- **Three endings:** the wall revealed with the answer circled; back to the opening mark, now corrected; the last tag flipped from a question to an answer, then the pull-back.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, title card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

# Caption News — our demo

One example among many. Don't reuse its story, arc, shots, props or timings.

Demo: *The Bee Ledger* (蜜蜂账本, 59.5 s) · `caption-news.mp4` · source in [`demo/`](demo/)

In 2025 America's beekeepers lost 1.3 million honey bee colonies, nearly half of what they started the year with. So are the bees running out? No: on January 1, 2026 there were 6 % more colonies than a year before, because the same beekeepers added 1.45 million. The film keeps the books in two columns — what died, what was rebuilt — and then explains the turn one fact per shot: how they rebuild, what hurts the colonies, the worst quarter, where it hit, and that they are still rebuilding. Every number is from one public report, USDA NASS *Honey Bee Colonies* (August 3, 2026), shown on screen.

This is an unofficial film made from real public material (USDA footage, photos and data; CC BY footage from Wikimedia Commons). The channel "简闻" is fictional; USDA did not make or endorse it.

## Story & structure

Shape: an inverted pyramid that turns at a quarter of the way in. Hook (0–5 s): the biggest number lands on frame 4 over rows of hives. Title sting (5–7.5 s). Setup (7.5–13 s): the loss as a proportion of the hives, then the viewer's question on a freeze frame, in silence. Turn (13–19 s): the report's own headline, highlighted — "Up 6 Percent" — and the count on a line chart, a text-only breath. Development (19–50 s): the ledger in two columns (lost vs added, counters racing), three ways to rebuild in a lit grid, the report's sentence on varroa mites and the mite itself under the electron microscope, the stressor ranking (a held judgement frame), the worst quarter (a spike on the loss line), the map (California) dissolving into an almond orchard through California's outline, and the rebuilding still going on. Ending (50–54.5 s): half a second of silence, then a two-part verdict on footage: "蜜蜂没有消失 / 是养蜂人在硬撑". End card (54.5–59.5 s).

Formats spent, each once and each for a new fact: cold-open number hook; title sting that becomes the channel bug; caption cards with yellow keywords (one line per language); rolling counters; source tag; per-shot footage credits; proportion-by-darkness sweep; freeze frame with brackets and timecode; document close-up with highlighter (twice: a headline, then a sentence, with a pull-quote mark); line chart (twice: stock, then loss rate); split screen; three-panel grid; punch-in with circle callout; ranked bar chart; choropleth map with push-in; mask transition from map to photo; lower third (place and date); text-only beat; end card.

## Score structure

- 120 BPM, 4/4. A minor (Am–F–G) for the hook; A minor groove after the sting; **hard stop** into silence at 10.5 (only the swarm's own buzz and the question), a suspended-cymbal swell from 12.15; the turn at 13.0 is a C-major brass chord with crash and glockenspiel; groove B in C major (C–G–Am–F) with vibraphone off-beats and claps under the turn, the chart breath (a glockenspiel figure, 16–19 s), the ledger and the grid (glockenspiel pings on the counters' arrival and each grid word); a thin bar of kick and spiccato cellos under the varroa document; the mite at 30.6 lands on timpani, bass drum and low trombones, then half-time D minor with cellos; a snare build (eighths → sixteenths) into the spike at 39.75 (crash + B♭ brass against A: the wrong chord on the worst number); toms and a cymbal swell under the map push, a crash on the mask; the groove returns, brighter, under the rebuilding; 0.5 s of silence; A major for the verdict at 50.5 (brass, horns, timpani, tubular bells); the end card holds horns and contrabass under a glockenspiel A–C♯–E–A and fades.
- Instruments: MuldjordKit drums, electric bass, marimba (a sixteenth-note ostinato: the hive's hum), vibraphone, glockenspiel, staccato trumpet and trombone, horn, timpani, bass drum, suspended cymbal, orchestral snare, claps, spiccato cellos, contrabass.
- Foley (procedural, `audio/mix.py` from `events.json`): chunk slams, counter rattles, whooshes into cards, highlighter squeaks, the camera shutter on the freeze, a stamp on "+6%", pops, map ticks, a riser into the map push, paper on each card.
- Natural sound: the swarm's own audio (Сарапулов, CC BY 4.0) low under the hook, alone under the freeze (J-cut 0.3 s before it), and under the verdict and end card.
- Mix: music about 10 dB under the voice and ducked; under speech the music also loses 1.2–5 kHz (the consonant band) — without it, speech-to-text heard "colonies" as "collins" in the full mix; −14.1 LUFS integrated.
- Voice: Kokoro `af_bella`, 12 lines, speed 1.0–1.17; numbers spelled out in the TTS text, digits in the captions.

## Palette & props

- Ink `#0E0E0C`, ivory `#F7F5EF`, honey `#FFC21A` (the point, gains, keywords, the bug), loss red `#FF4A3D`, label grey `#8D8B83`, the ledger sheet `#151512` with ruled lines and a red double margin.
- Type: Noto Sans SC 900 / 500, Inter Tight 800 / 500 / 600 italic (OFL subsets in `demo/fonts/`).
- Channel bug "简闻 | 蜜蜂账本 THE BEE LEDGER" (fictional channel).

## End card

From 54.5 s, held five seconds over the blurred, darkened hive entrance: "蜜蜂账本" (150 px), "The Bee Ledger" (honey), a thin rule, "CAPTION NEWS · 字幕新闻", "LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5", then five lines of sources: the data (USDA NASS report, its scope, and that 2025 losses and additions are four quarters summed), every CC BY work with title, author and licence, and the public-domain sources. The "LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5" sign-off belongs to this library's demo only; a user's film carries no LemoLab credit and no copy of this card.

Demo-specific choices and pitfalls: the hive-rows footage is Dutch (Altena TV) and is used only as "a box is a colony", never labelled as a US location; its station logo is cropped out and two hive stencils with a beekeeper's phone number are blurred. The almond photo is from 2014 and says so. The report's own wording sets the words: "stressor", not "killer"; "four quarters summed", not "annual net loss"; the report's page-1 figure for varroa in April–June 2026 (26.3 %) disagrees with its own table (22.2 %), so only January–March is used. A first draft spent a bar chart on "11–12 % every quarter" and later a line chart with the same quarters — the same fact twice; the bar chart was cut. Chart titles longer than six characters failed the reading check and were shortened; the California label was moved earlier so it holds 2.5 s before the push.

# Caption News — Style Prompt

> Social-video news that reads with the sound off. Real footage, photos and the source document are the ground; huge captions are the lead actor, slammed in a chunk at a time with one keyword on a yellow block. Hard cuts on a music grid, numbers that roll, a source tag that slides in whenever a figure appears, and the original document highlighted on screen before its number is believed. 16:9, built for a feed.
> References (grammar only): the captions-first social news of the mid-2010s (NowThis, AJ+), horizontal explainers that set big type over footage (Bloomberg Quicktake). Never copy their logos, fonts, colour ratios, idents or shots, and never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

1. **Sound-off first.** Every beat must be understood from the picture and the captions alone; the voice adds pace, not information.
2. **The caption is the shot.** One Chinese line, set huge, slammed in two or three chunks, one keyword in a yellow block; one English line under it. The footage is chosen to sit under the line.
3. **Evidence on screen.** Each number arrives with its source: a source tag slides in; key figures are first seen highlighted in the original document; per-shot footage credits sit in the corner like a news "Video:" tag.
4. **A hook on frame 4.** The film's largest number lands in the first 0.15 s and rolls to its value.
5. **One turn.** The bad-news hook is answered by a fact that changes its meaning; the rest of the film explains that turn, one new fact per shot.

Not **Data Storytelling** (charts are short inserts between footage, never the whole film, never a dashboard). Not a **TV news package** (no anchor, no lower-third ticker, no studio, no scrolling crawl). Not a keynote: no headers, no centred title-and-bullets, no page turns.

## 2. Frame and layout (1920×1080)

| Zone | Position | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Footage | full bleed | video, photo, document or data card; never a vertical frame pillar-boxed in the middle |
| Caption card | left aligned at x 120; Chinese baseline y ≈ 948, English baseline y ≈ 1014 | one line per language, never wrapped |
| Channel bug | top left, x 96 y 52, 46 px high | yellow block with a fictional channel name + topic in Chinese and English small caps |
| Source tag | under the bug, y 108, 36 px | white "来源" + dark label (`USDA NASS · 2026.08.03`, `… · 第 13 页`); only on data and document shots, slides in 0.2 s |
| Footage credit | top right, 19 px on a 50 % dark chip | `视频 作者 · CC BY 3.0`; every CC BY shot carries it |
| Lower third | x 120, y 742, 96 px high | yellow bar + label + one English line; for a place, date or speaker, never for the main sentence |

Under the caption: a bottom gradient (0 → 84 % from y 560) plus a soft dark radial from the bottom-left corner; a top gradient (55 % → 0 over 200 px) under the bug and the credit. Data cards use a lighter gradient that starts at y 820. Graphics and charts sit right of centre and bleed to the frame edge; their title and source sit top left, never centred.

Vertical 9:16 is a different layout, not a crop: put the caption under a 1080×1560 footage band (horizontal sources then scale ≤ 1.5×), stack the chunks on two lines there (the one-line rule is for 16:9 subtitles), and move the bug and source tag into the top safe area.

## 3. Editing grammar

- **Cuts on a 120 BPM half-beat grid** (every cut at a multiple of 0.5 s). Footage shots 1.5–3 s; data cards and documents 3–4.5 s; a shot that holds a comparison stays until every item has been fully on screen ≥ 2.5 s.
- **Captions cross cuts.** A caption can run over two shots (picture changes, words don't); captions change at most every ~2.5 s even when shots change every 1.5 s. Reading time, not shot length, sets the caption clock.
- **The order of a fact**: footage (feeling) → the number on a card → the document line that says it → the consequence. Never a number without its source tag in the same shot.
- **Transitions are few and fixed**: hard cut (default); a 1–2-frame white flash on the turn and on the freeze; a card sliding in from the right with speed streaks (0.18 s); a split screen opening from its divider; grid panels rising staggered (0.1 s apart); a punch-in (0.3 s ease-out to ~1.25×) on the culprit; a **mask transition** where a photo grows out of a map shape. No dissolves, no page turns, no 3D flips.
- **Pace**: a strong action within 0.5 s of every shot; no frame flat for more than 1 s (rolling counters, line drawing, highlighter sweeps, slow pushes keep it alive); one held breath (2–3 s) after the turn; two real silences.

## 4. Caption card (the subtitle *is* the graphic)

- **Chinese line**: Noto Sans SC 900, 88 px (verdict lines 110 px), ivory `#F7F5EF`, 20 px dark soft shadow. Split into 2–3 chunks with `|` in the timeline; each chunk slams 0.12 s after the previous: scale 1.3 → 1 in 0.13 s (back ease, overshoot 1.6), opacity full in 0.04 s.
- **Keyword**: `{…}` inside a chunk; a honey-yellow block `#FFC21A` wipes left → right in 0.12 s behind it, text turns ink `#0E0E0C`. One keyword per caption, at most.
- **English line**: Inter Tight 500, 33 px, ivory, fades and rises 10 px in 0.18 s, 0.1 s after the first chunk. It is the spoken line (numbers as digits), not a translation of the Chinese.
- **One line per language, always.** If either language would wrap, split the sentence into two captions. A caption is on screen ≥ 1.8 s and ideally ≥ the spoken line + 0.6 s; the Chinese is a paraphrase short enough to read in that time (≤ ~14 characters).
- The `.srt` is generated from the same timeline (`timeline.json` → `tools/cues.py` → `core/render/srt.py`): one Chinese line, one English line per cue.
- A text-only beat (caption with no voice) is native to the style: use it for the breath after the turn.

## 5. Graphics

- **Ledger card** (the data-card ground): `#151512` sheet, faint ruled lines every 54 px (4.5 % white), a thin red double margin at x 78/86 — the "account book" that ties every chart together. It slides in from the right over 0.18 s; inside, a slow push (×1.025–1.03 over the shot).
- **Colour meaning**: honey `#FFC21A` = the point / gains / the highlight; red `#FF4A3D` = losses, the spike, the bad number; ivory = everything else; grey `#8D8B83` = labels and units; `#5E5C55` = the bars that don't matter.
- **Numbers**: Inter Tight 800 with fixed-width digit cells (`num()` in `demo/main.js`), so a rolling counter never jitters. Counters roll with ease-out and turn their colour when they arrive. Units in Chinese (箱, 万箱) set smaller after the number.
- **Charts**: titled top left in Chinese (Noto Sans SC 900 64 px, ≤ 6 characters so it can be read in the shot) with one grey English line; lines draw segment by segment (eio); the key point gets a bigger dot, an expanding ring (0.7 s) and a block label; bars grow from the left one after another (first one slower and longer if it is the point).
- **Map**: state shapes from Natural Earth, projected (Albers), sequential fill in five steps of one hue, states without data in dark grey with a "未单列" legend swatch; the subject state outlined in yellow with a leader and a label; the map pushes in on it.
- **Documents**: the PDF page rendered at 220 dpi as white paper on a dark desk (±1–2° tilt, soft shadow, vignette), pushed in slowly; highlighter rectangles placed from `pdftotext -bbox` coordinates (1 pt = 3.0556 px), `multiply` blend, swept left → right in 0.3–0.5 s; the number read from it is re-set as a big yellow block beside the page. The printed text is picture; what must be read is re-set in type.
- **Split screen**: two halves with a 4 px yellow divider that drops first; the "bad" half desaturated, darkened and tinted red, the "good" half in full grade; a label block (Chinese + English word) and a counter in each; a shared stamp centred on the divider.
- **Grid**: three panels (632 px, 12 px gaps) rising staggered; each one lights up (yellow border, label turns yellow) on the word that names it; numbered 1–2–3.
- **Freeze frame**: the shot stops on a frame, a 0.14 s white flash, punch 1.0 → 1.12, saturation drops to 45 %, yellow corner brackets close in on the subject, a timecode chip with a pause mark appears top right.
- **Title sting**: a yellow ruled page (the ledger again, in yellow) wipes across the left 45 % over live footage; the title slams, the English title and a dateline chip follow; the page wipes off left and the title becomes the channel bug.

## 6. Grade and image quality

- One grade for every piece of footage: `contrast(1.07) saturate(0.92) brightness(0.98)` + a 6 % warm soft-light layer; documents 4 %. Light grain in the master (`mux.sh … 30 1`).
- **Scale limits**: modern footage ≤ 1.5× (prepare frames at their final size with ffmpeg: crop, lanczos, `unsharp=5:5:0.45`); photos ≤ 1:1 of their source; archive material ≤ 2.5× after deblocking. Pushes stay inside those limits — a 720p source already at 1.5× gets no push.
- Remove station logos by cropping (never cover them with a caption), blur legible private details (phone numbers, names on hives, number plates) with `delogo`, skip shots with burned-in text.
- Captions, numbers and charts are always vector, never scaled footage.

## 7. Sound palette

| Layer | What | Level |
|---|---|---|
| Voice | one brisk narrator (Kokoro, speed 1.1–1.17), numbers spelled out in the TTS text | compressed, ≈ 8 dB over the music |
| Music | 120 BPM pulse in sampled instruments: kit (kick on the beat, hats on off-beats), eighth-note electric bass, a sixteenth-note marimba ostinato, vibraphone off-beat chords, glockenspiel accents, staccato brass stabs on the big numbers, timpani and suspended cymbal for turns | ducked ~45 % under the voice |
| Structure | the hook hit on frame 4; a hard stop into silence before the turn (only natural sound and the question); the turn lands on a major-key brass hit; half-time and low strings for the threat; a snare build into the spike; a second short silence before the verdict; a major chord with bells on the verdict | |
| Foley | every graphic action has a sound: chunk slam (click + thump), counter rattle (a tick every 45 ms), whoosh into each card, highlighter squeak, camera shutter on the freeze, stamp thump on a big number, pops for labels, ticks as map states fill, a riser into the map push | |
| Natural sound | the subject's own location sound (here a swarm), J-cut 0.3 s before the freeze, bed under the ending | not ducked below audibility |

Master −14 LUFS, true peak −1.2 dB (`core/render/mux.sh`).

## 8. Native moves

1. **Frame-4 hook** — kicker line, then a giant number in a yellow block rolling to its value in 0.45 s, then the unit and the subject word (`hook()`).
2. **Chunk slam with one yellow keyword** (`capCard()`).
3. **Proportion by darkness** — a yellow line sweeps across the footage to the percentage; what it passed goes grey and dark; the figure appears on the dark side (`shotHalf()`). Works for any "X % of …".
4. **The document says it** — headline or sentence highlighted from PDF bbox coordinates, then the number popped as a yellow block beside the paper (`paper()`, `shotDoc6()`, `shotQuote()`).
5. **Freeze and question** — the image stops on the viewer's question, music cut to silence (`shotFreeze()`).
6. **Ledger split** — two counters racing side by side, the difference stamped after both settle (`shotSplit()`).
7. **Lit grid** — three ways / three causes, each panel lighting on its word (`shotGrid()`).
8. **Punch and circle** — 0.3 s punch-in on the culprit, a circle drawn round it, a leader to its name and its Latin name (`shotSem()`).
9. **Map to ground** — the map pushes into a region, then a photo of that place grows out of the region's outline (`shotMap()`).

## 9. Material

1. **Ask the user first** whether they have their own footage, photos, documents or data (and the rights to them). Their material comes first; the sources below are the fallback.
2. **Where to look** (judge every file on its own page, not the search result):
   - **Wikimedia Commons** (video and photos): read the licence on each file page. Fine: CC0, public domain, CC BY (credit author, title, licence on screen and in `CREDITS`). Not used: CC BY-SA, "no known restrictions", unclear licences, YouTube re-uploads, colourised or "restored" versions.
   - **U.S. federal agencies** (USDA, USGS, NASA, NOAA, NARA): works of federal employees are public domain; check that the page does not credit a contractor or a third party. NASA: https://images.nasa.gov. NARA: https://catalog.archives.gov.
   - **Internet Archive**: only items whose own page states public domain or a CC0/CC BY licence; U.S. works published before 1931 are public domain.
   - **Library of Congress**: read each item's rights statement; "no known restrictions" is not enough.
   - **Official documents and data** (reports, statistics, court filings) from the agency's own site: the source of every fact; keep `FACTS.md` (claim, URL, quoted wording, derived sums with their arithmetic).
   - **Map geometry**: Natural Earth (public domain).
3. **Before downloading, tell the user** what you will fetch, from where and under which licence, and keep within a size budget. The finder copied into this style, `demo/tools/footage.py` (`search commons|archive|nasa`, `fetch`, `used`, `md`), logs licence, author, page and the seconds used of each file into `SOURCES.jsonl` and writes `SOURCES.md`; `demo/tools/commons-tools/peek.py` previews a Commons video from thumbnails before downloading it, `seg.py` downloads only a segment of a long one, `commons_thumb.py` takes a standard-width thumbnail when the original is rate-limited. Wikimedia rate-limits bursts (HTTP 429): one request at a time with pauses.
4. **People on screen**: no close-up or slow motion of an identifiable private person; public figures and people in the news event are fine. Never use generated images as footage.

## 10. Engine

Copy `demo/` into the project and replace the content:
- `main.js` — the page (`window.render(t)` draws synchronously with placeholders first, so `TEXTS(t)` is valid for `readcheck.mjs`, then loads the frames it needs and draws again). Shot functions per format; `SHOTS` table for cuts.
- `timeline.json` — captions (`zh` with `|` chunks and `{keyword}`, `en`), voice start times, silences and hits; read by the page, `tools/cues.py` (.srt + timing check) and `audio/mix.py`.
- `tools/prep.sh` — every video shot as a 30 fps JPEG sequence at its display size (crop, lanczos, unsharp, delogo); report pages; photos; the map projection (`tools/map_prep.py`).
- `audio/mix.py` — sampled score from the timeline, foley from `events.json`, voice, natural sound, ducking.
- `tools/fonts.sh` (OFL subsets for every character in `main.js`), `tools/final_check.sh` (loudness, black frames, speech-to-text of the final mix).

## 11. Pitfalls

- **Text that can't be read in its shot.** Chart titles ≤ 6 Chinese characters; ornamental stamps (datelines) must recur readably elsewhere; a label that changes text (a counter) is reported to `TEXTS` with its final value. Run `readcheck.mjs`.
- **Two-line Chinese captions in 16:9** read as a slide. Split the sentence instead.
- **The voice running to the cut**: lines that end on the cut feel rushed; speed the TTS (≤ 1.17 — faster, Kokoro starts to mangle names: "varroa" became "Veroa") or shorten the line.
- **Homophones in ASR**: "requeen the weak" was heard as "week"; "varroa mite" as "might". Rewrite the line ("give old ones a new queen", "varroa mites").
- **Words stronger than the source**: the report says "stressor", not "killer"; quarterly losses summed are not "annual net loss". Write what the source says.
- **Footage from elsewhere**: illustrative footage (here Dutch hives) never carries a place label it doesn't have; dates on photos (an almond orchard in 2014) are stated in the credit.
- **Blank first frames on transitions**: start split/grid/sting animations 0.1–0.15 s before the cut so frame 1 already has picture.
- **Station logos**: crop them out; never park a caption over a logo.

## 12. Variation space

The agent decides per film: topic, the turn, which formats are spent where, footage, the channel's fictional name and colour (keep one accent colour), the title.

- **Three structures:** the inverted pyramid with a mid-film turn (bad number → "really?" → the document says otherwise → why); a list of three that turns on the third; a countdown of numbers that ends on the one that matters.
- **Three openings:** the biggest number on frame 4; the document headline highlighted in the first second; a freeze on the event with a question.
- **Three endings:** a two-part verdict caption on footage with music returning after a silence; back to the hook's number, now re-read; the last data card's key point becoming the closing caption.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

# 80s Cel Anime — our demo

One example among many. Don't reuse its story, arc, shots, props or timings.

Demo: *City Lights, 1987* (59 s) · `cel-anime-80s.mp4` · source in [`demo/`](demo/)


## Story & structure

After the rain, a courier nicknamed "Nightbird" rides a white motorbike across a neon city to deliver a pilot's forgotten cassette to the launch pad before a dawn rocket launch. One hero, one goal, one deadline (sunrise).

Arc (59 s): cold open with a deadline → the hero sets off (title hit) → joyful momentum montage → an obstacle (a drawbridge rising) → one decisive move (the jump; the peak *freezes*) → release into a new light (night becomes dawn) → end card. The song on the tape is the score itself: when the cassette plays aboard, the score becomes diegetic.

How the old guide phrased the adaptation idea for this story (kept as one example, not a rule): turn a topic into a delivery, a race against a deadline or a launch; plant the goal early (the rocket on the horizon), block it in act two, reveal it in the light at the end. Other adaptations it listed: a product launch as a courier racing the product to the stage; a love story as two lights crossing a sleeping city; a history lesson as a pilot flying through eras painted as backgrounds.

Native powers spent: painted city vs flat cel (neon city, wet asphalt, dawn sky), limited animation (held close-ups, the jump as a painted still), backlit light (signs, tail lights, gauges, title), speed grammar (parallax, speed lines, impact frames), the theme song as a plot object (the cassette).

## Shots

| Beat | Camera |
|---|---|
| Cold open | **Multiplane crane-down** over a tall painted plate (sky → rooftops → neon → street), foreground layers faster; radio dispatch over rain |
| The object that matters | Tight insert on a gloved hand holding the cassette, soft bokeh behind, a highlight sliding over its plastic |
| Resolve | Extreme close-up on the eyes; they open in three 8 fps drawings on the line "Copy. I'll beat the sun." |
| Title | Backlit title card, letters flicker on at 12 fps, a light bar sweeps across, star glint, on the brass hit |
| Momentum | Side tracking with 4 parallax layers + tail-light trail; rear view into a neon canyon (pseudo-3D); held bust with neon light bands; wheel insert through a puddle; a wide elevated-highway shot that **plants the goal** (the rocket across the bay) |
| Obstacle | First-person approach to the rising drawbridge; glove twisting the throttle and the rev gauge in extreme close-up, cutting faster |
| Peak | Low front view on radial speed lines → one-beat freeze + white flash → impact frame → painted "harmony" still of the airborne bike with a slow pan → impact frame → landing with sparks and camera shake |
| Release | The same side-tracking composition as the night ride, repainted at dawn by the sea with the sky open |
| Handover | Two hands through a fence pass the tape; a finger presses PLAY on the cockpit cassette deck |
| Ending | The rocket lifts off (tilt up, delayed); warm close-up that answers the opening line ("Told you I'd beat the sun."), then the end card |

The rider's front view was tucked behind a tinted windscreen so only goggles and hair show, letting the headlight flare carry the shot. Cuts landed on bars (116 BPM, bar = 2.069 s).

## Score structure

Original city-pop / synth-funk "anime opening", synthesized in numpy (`demo/music/score.py`): 116 BPM, E♭ major, maj7/9 chords, the J-pop "royal road" progression (IVM7–V7–iii7–vi7). FM electric piano (DX7-style 1:1 carriers + a 14:1 bell transient), slap bass (thumb + octave pops), gated-reverb snare, synth brass stabs, chorus-y 16th-note guitar chanks, string pad, a singable lead hook, FM bell sparkle, and a **key change up a semitone** for the last chorus.

Written to the cut: intro under the cold open, a fill bar with space for engine revs, the title on a brass hit, verse under the montage, a pre-chorus build, **one beat of true silence** before the jump, the chorus on the painted still, an accent on the landing, and the final chord on the end card. Diegetic twist: when the tape plays in the cockpit, the score is band-passed to a cassette sound for one bar, then opens to full range with the key change as the rocket lifts.

Foley: engine from an RPM curve (harmonic saw stack + firing jitter + band-passed exhaust pulses, low-passed when airborne), rain bed + random drops, tire hiss on wet road, wind, bridge bells, radio squelch clicks, impact boom, metal scrape and sparks, cassette clicks, button + motor, rocket ignition and roar.

Voices: an English-dub feel, 8 short lines: the heroine (Kokoro `af_bella`) and a radio dispatcher (Kokoro `am_michael` through a band-pass 380–2800 Hz + saturation + squelch). Whisper misheard "Launch is at dawn", so it became "The launch is at dawn". Mix: voices balanced by RMS ~10 dB above the ducked music, music ducked ~9 dB under lines, engine and ambience ducked 3 dB, chorus 4–6 dB louder than the intro, two-pass loudnorm to −14 LUFS.

## Palette & props

- Night: indigo / deep violet / neon magenta / cyan / warm window gold. Dawn: periwinkle / rose / peach / pale gold. The hero's accent: a **coral scarf**, readable in both.
- Colour-model multipliers used: night lit ×[.78,.74,1.0], shadow ×[.58,.52,.92]; dawn lit ×[1.04,.9,.84]; a backlit silhouette set (dark purple with an orange rim) for the jump. Skin line ≈ `#5a2e2e`.
- Props: white motorbike, cassette labelled "SIDE A · CITY LIGHTS", headset and goggles (near-black, heavier lines), pinch-grip gloves, rev gauge, drawbridge with red warning lights, rocket on a floodlit pad across the bay, cockpit cassette deck with backlit level meters. Signs: BAR, CAFE, 喫茶, ホテル, カラオケ.
- The heroine, as built in `head80.js`: eyes at the vertical middle of the head, mouth at the upper third between nose base and chin; iris layered top-dark band → dark upper half → main colour → bright lower crescent, one large and one small highlight; 2–3 separate lashes in the flick; mouth set closed / set / talk / "oh" / pant / smile / open smile with a dark-red interior and a faint lower-lip stroke; profile with a small skull-back, small slightly upturned nose, neck leaning forward. Blinks hold the closed drawing 2–3 frames; brows carry resolve vs exhaustion; shoulders rise when panting; a star glint in the eye highlight on a musical accent.
- CRT numbers used: chroma blur ~7 px, Cr shift ~2 px; scanlines 3 px period, strength 0.18, gap `1 − a·ph·(1 − 0.6·L)`; grille ±0.06; phosphor glow 0.35; corners `1 − 0.28·(2u²v² + 0.25(u²+v²))`. Moiré check: at 720p the 3 px scanline becomes a clean 2-row alternation; 900p shows a faint 5-row pattern; below 480p it disappears. Film-only artefacts (gate weave, dust, scratches, misregistration) were tried in the treatment and removed: they contradict the tape conceit. The power-on opens the film with a thunk + line whine; tracking noise marks the tape beat with a short hiss/warble.

## End card

Darkened final dawn background, the title, the style name "80s Cel Anime", "LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5", a one-line originality note and credits. The "LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5" sign-off belongs to this library's demo only; a user's film carries no LemoLab credit and no copy of this card.

Title card as used: "CITY LIGHTS" in heavy italic chrome with シティ・ライツ above (Dela Gothic One), a red "1987" and a spaced-out tagline. Subtitles: Barlow Semi Condensed 600, 54 px, cream-yellow `#fff0a0`, 9 px dark outline, 96 px above the bottom; radio lines cyan `#8ff4ff` with a boxed "● BASE" tag; each line up for max(duration + 0.6 s, 1.9 s).

## Rights & credits

- Original score, sound design, animation and all drawings: generated by code in this folder (numpy, Canvas 2D, WebGL). No samples, no stock art.
- Voices: Kokoro TTS (Apache 2.0), voices `af_bella`, `am_michael`.
- Fonts (SIL Open Font License 1.1, licence files in `demo/fonts/`): Dela Gothic One (artakana), Kanit (Cadson Demak), Barlow Semi Condensed (Jeremy Tribby).
