# Swiss Motion Graphics — our demo

One example among many. Don't reuse its story, arc, shots, props or timings.

Demo: *Five Rules for a Poster* (44 s) · `swiss-motion.mp4` · source in [`demo/`](demo/)


A 30–60 second film: five rules build one concert poster on a grid; a red circle breaks the grid, and the poster turns out to be the score of the music. The demo sets Archivo as its one family.

## Story & structure

Pure 2D graphic design animated on a grid: flat white paper, black type and bars, a very light grey and **one** saturated red. It is the language of 1950s–70s Zurich concert posters (Müller-Brockmann, Hofmann, Gerstner, Crouwel) turned into motion the way modern identity systems move (Experimental Jetset, Pentagram): **every element snaps to the grid, every move lands on a beat, nothing bounces**.

The charm is **rigor with one exception**. The whole frame obeys a system, so the one element that doesn't obey it becomes a character.

Never copy a specific historical poster's composition (no concentric-circle or fan compositions lifted from Müller-Brockmann). Don't use Helvetica or Akzidenz font files. Pick an OFL neo-grotesque (Archivo, Inter, Schibsted Grotesk, Instrument Sans…). Never name a real institution on a poster.

Pick stories where **the system itself tells the story**. The demo used all five native powers, the strongest (the grid means something) at the peak:

| Native power | Story use |
|---|---|
| **The modular grid** | The grid is the stage and the rulebook. Show it being built (lines draw on the beat), show it briefly in section gaps, and at the peak **make the grid mean something**: in the demo, 7 columns = the 7 notes of A dorian and 16 rows = 16 eighth notes, so the poster *is* the score. |
| **Snap = beat** | Every element's arrival is a percussion hit: type clack, knife, ruling pen. Picture and music share one coordinate system, not a sync pass after the fact. |
| **Rules generate design (programme)** | The plot is a set of rules applied one by one to one artifact. End by showing the same programme generating many artifacts (the Gerstner reveal). |
| **Extreme scale contrast** | A 700 px numeral next to 19 px technical notes. The giant element is the chapter card, the tiny one is texture. |
| **One signal colour** | Only one thing is red, so red = the protagonist. When it breaks a rule it is the only thing on screen that is not exact. |

**Adapting any topic:** turn it into **a system plus one exception**. A product launch: the product's spec sheet assembles on a grid, then one feature breaks out of it. A company's history: each decade is a rule added to one poster. A love story: two red elements on two different grids, and the film ends when one of them leaves its grid.

**Emotional arc (30–60s):** order being built (curious, crisp) → order complete (correct and a bit dull, *say it*) → hesitation (the red element twitches and snaps back) → the break (the only non-snapped, linear move in the film; drums drop out) → everything else re-flows around it, better (full band back) → the reveal (the grid means something) → scale reveal (same system, many outputs) → back to the hero artifact on the end card.

## Shots

The "camera" is a 2D matrix (centre, scale, rotation). It moves only with the precise ease and only on beats.

| Beat | Camera |
|---|---|
| Opening | Locked full frame. One gesture: a red line strikes across and the grid columns grow out of it on sixteenths |
| Building (rules) | Locked spread, so the viewer reads cause (rule, left) → effect (artifact, right) |
| The break | Left page slides out, artifact moves to centre-left, grid lines extend across the whole frame (the grid is bigger than the page) |
| Reveal | **Rotate the artifact 90° in 1.5 beats and stop.** Only then do labels (note names, bar numbers) wipe in, then the playhead sweeps two bars. Each bar turns red on the exact frame of its onset: put onsets on whole frames (multiples of 0.25 s at 24 fps) |
| Scale reveal | Rotate back while pulling out to a wall of artifacts from the same system |
| Ending | The red line strikes again and cuts the other artifacts away. Push back to the opening spread, end card on the left page, hero artifact on the right |

- **Two curves only.** Precise ease `cubic-bezier(.7,0,.2,1)` for snaps, linear for lines being drawn, the playhead and the rule-breaker. No overshoot, no spring, no bounce.
- **Durations are note values** at the film's BPM (120: 1/8 = 0.25 s, 1/16 = 0.125 s). A snap starts one note value early and **lands on the beat**.
- **Entrances are wipes or clip-reveals, never fades.** Words rise out of a clip rect from below the baseline (1/16 note) and leave upward (1/8 note). Lines grow along their length. Paper appears by a vertical wipe. Big numerals climb in **4 eased steps** ("one module at a time").
- **Deletions are knife cuts.** A 2 px line crosses the element in 1/16, then the element collapses vertically to its midline in 1/8.
- **Ripples are ordered by distance** from the cause. After the red circle lands, units re-flow two at a time on sixteenths, nearest first.
- **The exception moves differently.** It is linear, not snapped, and pauses for one eighth mid-flight (a glance back). It grows as it travels. A coordinate readout next to it turns from `col 5.00 row 0.00 · on grid` to red `off grid` with non-integer (even negative) values.
- Everything renders at a smooth 24 fps. There's no stepping: this style is digital precision, not hand-made.

## Score structure

- **Music**: Motorik / krautrock, 120 BPM, A dorian (not a generic piano-and-strings bed). Layer one instrument per rule:
  1. hats only;
  2. + full motorik kit (`drum_kit`: kick 1, 3, 3&; snare 2, 4; closed hat eighths);
  3. + `electric_bass` eighth-note root pulse;
  4. + numpy saw arpeggio sixteenths with an opening filter;
  5. + `glockenspiel` doubled by a soft numpy square lead.

  **Drop the drums for the one bar of the break**, return on the landing. Before the reveal add one bar of near-silence (bass pedal + quarter-note tick). During the reveal keep only kick + bass + melody so every note is audible.
- **The melody comes from the same JSON as the picture** (`score.json`: column → pitch, row → onset, length → duration). "The poster is the score" is true in code, not faked.
- **Foley follows materials**, dry and close, no reverb:
  - letterpress clack (metal transient + 3.3 / 5.1 kHz resonances + wooden tray);
  - ruling pen "tss";
  - guillotine (band-pass sweep + metal snick);
  - paper slap / slide;
  - numeral "thunk" per step;
  - block snap;
  - circle landing (58 Hz felt thump).

  The rule-breaker is the only element that *sings*: a sine glide that follows its position.
- **Voice**: cool, crisp female narrator, Kokoro `af_sarah` at speed 1.0. It had ~7× the 3–8 kHz consonant energy of `af_kore`. Keep lines rule-like: "Rule one. Build a grid." Check every line with whisper (write numbers as `"asr": "Rule 1, …"`).
- **Mix**: voice compressed, music ducked ~−10 dB under voice (voice ≥ 6 dB above music), −14 LUFS.

## Palette & props

- **Frame grid**: 1920×1080, 12 columns, 96 px side margins, 24 px gutters (122 px columns), 24 px baseline. Treat the frame as a **spread**: left page (cols 1–6) = the "programme" (numeral, rule text, notes); right page (cols 8–12) = the artifact (poster 706×1008, ratio 0.70 ≈ Swiss world format).
- **Artifact grid**: derive it from the content (Gerstner). In the demo the poster has 7 columns × 91 px and 16 rows × 40 px, with a 26 px baseline grid in the text zone. I first tried 12 semitone columns: bars were only 43 px wide and the poster looked like a data chart. **Choose module sizes that give the bars mass.**
- **Palette**: page `#EAE9E5`, paper `#FFFFFF`, ink `#111111`, signal red `#E30613`, grid lines `#CFCEC9` on the page / `#C9C8C2` while building / `#E2E1DC` on paper, secondary bars `#CFCEC9`. No gradients, no shadows, no particles, no grain (mux grain 0).
- **Type**: one family for the whole film (demo: **Archivo** variable, weights 400–800). Letter-spacing −2.2% at ≥ 90 px. Lowercase headlines (`neue musik`). Rule numerals at ~980 px (700 px figure height), bottom-aligned with the poster's bottom edge, **optically** flush left (subtract the glyph's left bearing). Notes 19 px Medium. Always `document.fonts.load` every weight before drawing.
- **Composition**: flush left, ragged right. Everything on a grid line. Big white spaces are part of the layout. The final composition must be **visibly bolder** than the "correct" one:
  - one main diagonal with a strong long-short rhythm;
  - the red element at ~2× scale;
  - elements **bleeding** off the paper edge;
  - type overprinting the red circle (black on red).
  Merely tilting the correct layout is not enough.
- **Bars as notes**: bar width = column minus 8 px; consecutive cells of one note merge into one bar (overdraw 1 px at the seams or antialiasing shows hairlines, especially when rotated).
- **The secondary voice** (bass) is light-grey bars under the black ones. They read as a shadow diagonal and give depth without a second colour.

## Titles, subtitles & end card

- **Subtitles are part of the layout**, not a bar at the bottom. Each line sits at column 1 on the spread's left page: the first sentence as a 30 px Medium grey lead-in, the rest as a 76 px Bold statement. Each word clip-reveals on its whisper timestamp. Non-rule lines use Regular weight ("Perfect. And a little dull."). In other shots the line sits at column 1 of that shot, at the artifact's headline baseline or under the wall like a museum label.
- **Title card**: `Five Rules / for a Poster`, 120 px Bold, two lines flush left, sitting on the opening red line. A 19 px caption row with a 1 px rule above it (`A programme in five steps · 1961 · ♩ = 120`).
- **Caption row + notes**: top of the left page (title / `Rule 0n / 05` / keyword); bottom of column 5: 2–3 technical notes per rule (`Columns 7 · Rows 16 · Module 91 × 40`). Bottom of column 7: a bar counter `bar 04.3`.
- **End card**: the opening spread again. `Swiss Motion / Graphics` 120 px, red line under it, `LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5` 36 px, notes at the bottom, hero poster on the right. The LemoLab sign-off belongs to this library's demo only: a user's film carries no LemoLab credit and no copy of this card.

## Pitfalls we hit (demo record)

- **12 columns looked like a chart.** Grid modules must give the graphic elements mass. We used fewer, wider columns for the artifact and kept the standard 12 columns for the frame.
- **The "better" composition wasn't obviously better.** Four small staircases → one scattered layout wasn't convincing. Fix: one main diagonal with long/short rhythm, 2× red element, bleeds, type over red.
- **Rotation reveal needs a stop.** Rotating and labelling at the same time read as noise. Order it: rotate (1.5 beats) → hold → grid lines → labels → playhead → sweep.
- **Merged bars showed seams** after rotation and scaling (antialiasing between adjacent rects). Overdraw 1 px where cells join.
- **Labels overlapping the header**: hide the caption row before the rotated shot.
- **Word timings**: whisper splits or merges words ("type face"), and `asr_check` reports the first word at −0.6 s (padding). Align by letters and clamp to 0 (`tools/words.py`).
- **Subtitle rule** (≥ voice + 0.6 s and ≥ 1.8 s): two lines missed by 2 ms. `tools/subs.py` asserts it, so fix by nudging start times.
- **The wall cut must follow the line**: shrink the wall board from the side the red line enters, in screen space.
- The other posters on the wall share the camera matrix, so draw them **only** during the wall shot. Otherwise they leak into other shots at ±786 px.
- Canvas `letterSpacing` also affects `measureText`, so compute widths after setting the font.

## Build notes

```
styles/swiss-motion/demo/
  score.json  grid = score: stiff / final melody, bass, circle, bleeds, timeline
  ease.js     cubic-bezier(.7,0,.2,1), snap(t, t_arrive, dur), steps(), track()
  film.js     layout system, rules, poster, circle, reveal, wall, end card, foley events
  main.js     loads fonts, score, lines, whisper word times; ?nosub=1, ?poster=1
  lines.json  voice script (af_sarah)          tools/words.py  word timings → subtitle reveal
  music/score.py  motorik score from score.json   mix.py  foley + ducked voice + music
  tools/subs.py   subtitle intervals (asserted) → srt     build.sh  one-shot rebuild
```

1. Design the layout system first: frame grid, artifact grid, what columns and rows *mean*. Write `score.json`.
2. `node core/render/still.mjs styles/swiss-motion/demo --range 0.5:43.5:1 --out …` then `sheet.py`. Review a 1 s overview plus dense 0.25 s strips around the break and each transition.
3. `tts.py` → `asr_check.py` (0 mismatches) → `tools/words.py`.
4. `music/score.py` (onsets from `score.json`; check sweep onsets ≤ 5 ms) → `events.mjs` → `mix.py` (prints voice/music/foley dB per line).
5. `video.mjs --workers 3` (1056 frames in ~12 s) → `mux.sh … 24 0`. Or simply `sh styles/swiss-motion/demo/build.sh` (~55 s from zero).

# Swiss Motion Graphics — Style Prompt

> International Typographic Style in motion: a modular grid, one typeface, one signal colour, and movement as exact as a printing press.
> References (grammar only): 1950s–70s Zurich posters (Müller-Brockmann, Hofmann, Gerstner, Crouwel) for the grid, flush-left type, scale contrast and "designing programmes"; modern identity systems in motion (Experimental Jetset, Pentagram) for snaps on the beat. Never copy a specific historical poster's composition (no concentric-circle or fan layouts lifted from Müller-Brockmann), never use Helvetica or Akzidenz font files, never name a real institution on a poster.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

- **Pure 2D graphic design animated on a grid**: flat paper, black type and bars, a very light grey and **one** saturated signal colour.
- **Every element snaps to the grid, every move lands on a beat, nothing bounces.**
- **Rigor with one exception**: the whole frame obeys a system, so the one element that doesn't becomes a character.
- **Extreme scale contrast**: a giant numeral next to tiny technical notes.

Not a keynote (no gradients, no glow, no device renders), not kinetic typography for a lyric video (words don't fly, spin or bounce), not data visualisation (bars have mass as graphic form, not as charted quantities, unless the grid gives them that meaning), not a Bauhaus pastiche of primary shapes.

## 2. Materials & rendering

- **Frame grid**: 1920×1080, 12 columns, ~96 px side margins, 24 px gutters, 24 px baseline. The frame can act as a **spread**: a left page (the programme: numeral, rule text, notes) and a right page (the artifact).
- **Artifact grid** derived from the content (Gerstner): what the columns and rows *mean* is a design decision. **Choose module sizes that give the elements mass**; too many thin columns make a layout look like a chart.
- **Surfaces**: page, paper, ink, signal colour, grid lines in two or three light greys (on page, while building, on paper). No gradients, no shadows, no particles, no grain (mux grain 0).
- **Bars and blocks** are flat rects; consecutive cells of one unit merge into one bar, overdrawn 1 px at seams (antialiasing shows hairlines, especially when rotated or scaled).
- **A secondary voice** can be light-grey elements under the black ones: depth without a second colour.
- **A 2D camera matrix** (centre, scale, rotation) for all moves.

## 3. Colour logic

- **Paper, ink, greys, and one signal colour.** Only one thing carries the signal colour; that makes it the protagonist. It is the only thing allowed to be inexact.
- Overprint is allowed: black type on the signal colour.
- The signal colour can be red, orange, ultramarine or green; choose it for the topic, then never add a second.
- Examples: `#EAE9E5` page, `#FFFFFF` paper, `#111111` ink, signal `#E30613`; or `#F2F0EA` / `#141414` / signal `#FF5A00`; or `#E9ECEF` / `#0B0B0B` / signal `#1F3FFF`.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- **One family for the whole film**, an OFL neo-grotesque (Archivo, Inter, Schibsted Grotesk, Instrument Sans…), several weights. Letter-spacing ~−2 % at ≥ 90 px. Headlines can be lowercase. Load every weight with `document.fonts.load` before drawing.
- **Flush left, ragged right**; everything on a grid line; big white space is part of the layout. Giant numerals are **optically** flush left (subtract the glyph's left bearing).
- **Subtitles are part of the layout**, not a bar at the bottom: each line sits at a column start in the current composition (a small grey lead-in + a large bold statement, or a caption like a museum label), each word clip-revealed on its whisper timestamp. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s); assert it in code.
- **Caption rows**: small (~19 px) medium-weight notes with a 1 px rule above; technical notes in a corner (module sizes, counts, a bar counter).

## 5. Motion quality

- **Two curves only**: a precise ease `cubic-bezier(.7,0,.2,1)` for snaps; linear for lines being drawn, playheads and the exception. No overshoot, no spring, no bounce.
- **Durations are note values** at the film's tempo. A snap starts one note value early and **lands on the beat**.
- **Entrances are wipes or clip-reveals, never fades**: words rise out of a clip rect from below the baseline and leave upward; lines grow along their length; paper appears by a wipe; big numerals climb in eased steps ("one module at a time").
- **Deletions are knife cuts**: a thin line crosses the element, then the element collapses to its midline.
- **Ripples are ordered by distance** from their cause, a couple of units per subdivision.
- **The exception moves differently**: linear, unsnapped, perhaps pausing mid-flight; a coordinate readout beside it can turn from "on grid" to "off grid".
- Smooth 24 fps, no stepping: digital precision, not hand-made.

## 6. Camera grammar

A vocabulary, not a route. The camera moves only with the precise ease and only on beats. Opening and ending come from the topic.

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Locked spread | cause (left) → effect (right) | a rule applied; a before/after; a comparison |
| Hard pan by one page or column | the next step in a system | a sequence; a catalogue; a timeline |
| Rotate 90° and stop | the same thing read another way | a poster as a score; a chart as a map |
| Pull out to a wall of artifacts | one programme, many outputs | a brand system; a product range; a series |
| Push into one module | detail; the unit of the system | a pixel; a letter; a single data point |
| Grid extends past the page | the system is bigger than the artifact | scale; ambition; a break from constraints |
| Split frame into equal cells | parallel cases | options; variants; team members |
| Vertical scroll through a column | reading; a list | a manifesto; a spec sheet; a timetable |

Framing: everything on the grid; the signal element may sit off-grid only when it is being the exception. Transitions are wipes, knife cuts, camera moves and re-flows; never dissolves.

## 7. Sound palette

- **Music with a grid of its own**: a steady pulse whose subdivisions give snap durations. Options: motorik / krautrock kit and bass, minimal techno, marimba or vibraphone patterns, a mechanical piano ostinato, a drum machine with a glockenspiel; one instrument added per new rule is a clear build.
- **Picture and music can share one data file** (a column → pitch, a row → onset), so a graphic can literally be the score.
- **Techniques (options)**: drop the drums for the one moment of the exception; a near-silent bar before a reveal; thin the band during a reveal so every note is audible.
- **Foley follows the materials of print**, dry and close, no reverb: letterpress clack, ruling pen "tss", guillotine snick, paper slap and slide, numeral thunk, block snap, felt thump for a landing, rubber stamp, typewriter carriage.
- **The exception can be the only element that sings** (a sine glide following its position).
- **Silence**: a hard stop of everything on a downbeat; the next snap reads as an event.
- **Mix**: voice compressed and ≥ 6 dB above music, music ducked ~10 dB under voice, −14 LUFS.
- **Voice**: cool, crisp, rule-like sentences; prefer voices with bright consonants.

## 8. Native moves

A menu: use the ones your story needs.

- **The grid means something.** Columns and rows become a quantity (notes, hours, floors, years). *Fits content like:* a building's floors and rooms; a week's timetable; a city's districts.
- **Snap = beat.** Every arrival is a percussion hit. *Fits content like:* a product's feature list; the steps of a recipe; a countdown.
- **Programme.** Rules applied one by one to one artifact, then the same programme generating many. *Fits content like:* a brand identity; a typeface family; a set of stamps.
- **Extreme scale contrast.** A giant element as chapter card beside tiny notes. *Fits content like:* a record statistic; a year; a price.
- **The exception.** One element breaks the grid, linear and unsnapped. *Fits content like:* an inventor; an outlier in the data; a rebel employee.
- **Knife cut.** An element deleted by a line. *Fits content like:* budget cuts; editing a text; removing a feature.
- **Re-flow.** Everything else rearranges around a change, nearest first. *Fits content like:* a team reorganised; traffic after a road closes; a layout adapting to a phone.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- Too many thin columns look like a chart → fewer, wider modules.
- A "better" composition that isn't obviously better → one strong diagonal with long/short rhythm, a larger signal element, bleeds, type over colour. Merely tilting is not enough.
- Rotating and labelling at once reads as noise → rotate, hold, then add labels.
- Merged bars show seams after rotation → overdraw 1 px.
- Elements that share the camera matrix leak into other shots → draw them only when on screen.
- Canvas `letterSpacing` affects `measureText` → measure after setting the font.
- Onsets that fall between frames flicker → put visual onsets on whole frames.
- Whisper splits or merges words and pads the first word → align by letters, clamp to 0.

## 10. Engine

In `demo/`: `ease.js` (`cubic-bezier(.7,0,.2,1)`, `snap(t, t_arrive, dur)`, `steps()`, `track()`), `film.js` (layout system, clip-reveal text, knife cuts, bars from a score, rotation reveal, wall of artifacts, caption rows), `main.js` (fonts, whisper word times, `?nosub=1`, `?poster=1`), `score.json` (the shared data file for picture and music), `tools/words.py` and `tools/subs.py` (word timings, asserted subtitle intervals). File list and build steps: [DEMO.md](DEMO.md) "Build notes".

## 11. Variation space

You decide the system, what the grid means, the exception (or none), the signal colour, the opening and the ending. All far from our demo:

- Structures: **a timetable** (a 24-row grid of hours fills with the topic's day, one row per beat); **an alphabet** (A to Z, each letter a module of the topic, the grid completing as a specimen sheet); **a comparison** (two systems side by side on a split spread until one element crosses the gutter).
- Openings: **a single dot** placed on the page, then the grid growing from it; **the finished artifact** that is then dismantled into its rules; **a giant numeral** filling the frame, which turns out to be a detail of a small layout.
- Endings: **the empty grid** after every element has been cut away; **a single word** flush left in the corner; **the exception leaves the frame** and the system closes over the space it left.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

# Exploded Teardown — our demo

One example among many. Don't reuse its story, arc, shots, props or timings.

Demo: *21 Keys, Opened* 《二十一键》 (38.75 s) · `teardown.mp4` · source in [`demo/`](demo/)

One half of the open-source Corne v4 split keyboard (foostan/crkbd, CC BY 4.0 / MIT), built from the project's own KiCad board, switch-plate file, case STEP, bill of materials and build guide. Chinese on screen, English narration, bilingual subtitles (Chinese line above, English below). Every number on screen and in the voice is in [`demo/FACTS.md`](demo/FACTS.md). The project's name and logo are not shown in the picture (only in the end-card credit line); the chip and part numbers are component designations from the BOM, and no package top carries a marking. This is an unofficial film made from the project's published files; the Corne project and its author (foostan) did not make or endorse it.

## Story & structure

Logline: twenty-one keys look like one object; opened, they are six layers drawn in public files, down to the chip, the lights and the sockets; closed again, every size on them is a published number.

Arc: touch (a grazing macro over the keycaps, one real keystroke) → the opening (one orbit, layers lift top first, keys in a wave, six labels) → inside (a dive into the room between the board and the case, looking up at the back of the board: the RP2040, the flash, a reverse-mounted LED; then a rise through the plate to the switch pins) → back together (a fast pull back, bottom-first closing, keys land with their stroke) → the numbers on the object (key pitch, width, depth, height as dimension lines) → end card.

Native moves spent: *one real keystroke* in the opening; *the wave lift* at the separation; *inside the gap* and *the leader that lands on the part* for the three stops; *lights on inside* at the LED; *dimensions drawn on the thing* before the card.

## Shots

One continuous camera. Times in seconds; 96 BPM, bar = 2.5 s.

| # | Time | Shot | Camera | Native move / note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.0–2.5 | keycap tops, the orange 1.5u key in the foreground, a soft light gliding across | grazing macro dolly, eye 33 mm above the floor, lens 30° | hook: material, a light sweep |

| 4 | 5.0–7.5 | keys rise in a wave from the back-left corner, then switches, plate, board, spacers, case; feet stay on the floor | orbit −31° → −9°, pulls back to 432 mm, model slides left (view offset 170 px) | the wave lift; hit at 5.0 |

| 13 | 33.75–38.75 | end card on the left, the keyboard turning on the right | drift az 40° → 59°, view offset −230 px | |

## Score structure

96 BPM, 4/4, D (Dm9 – B♭maj7 – F – C/E per bar), D major on the card. Every hit sits on a beat or half-beat of `src/timeline.js`.

| Section | Time | Palette | Notes |

| Touch | 0–4.4 | marimba in 8ths (soft), bowed vibraphone, room tone | the keystroke: switch click + low thock + return clack |
| Silence 1 | 4.4–5.0 | room tone, a filtered-noise suck | |
| Opening | 5.0–12.5 | marimba 16ths, electric bass, synth kick on 1 and 3, claves on 2 and 4, closed hi-hat 16ths | 21 plastic ticks in the wave, swooshes per layer, a ring for the brass, a thud for the case, a tick per label |
| Inside | 12.5–24.4 | bowed vibraphone chords, glass motif, pedal hi-hat in 8ths, sub kick once a bar | glockenspiel pings on each stop (A5, D6, E6), an arpeggio for the lights |
| Silence 2 | 24.6–25.0 | room tone only | |
| Closing | 25.0–33.75 | groove returns, four on the floor | 21 key landings (clack + click), board taps, the case thud; a pen hiss per dimension |
| Card | 33.75–38.75 | D-major marimba roll, bowed vibraphone D–F♯–A, bass D, glockenspiel answers | long tail |

Mix (`demo/mix.py`): voice compressed and about 8–10 dB over the music while it speaks (music ducked 55 % on the voice envelope), music high-passed at 44 Hz, foley at 36 Hz; loudest moments in order: the landings (26.6), the card, the pull back (25.0), the opening hit (5.0). 二十一键 (Noto Sans SC 500), *21 Keys, Opened* (Inter Light), `产品拆解 · EXPLODED TEARDOWN`, `CAD：foostan/crkbd · CC BY 4.0`, `LemoLab × Claude Opus 5.5`, an orange rule; the closed keyboard drifting on the right. 5 s. ```

```
  index.html        WebGL canvas + 2D marks canvas, fonts
  src/timeline.js   the single timeline: beats, layer timings, gaps, narration, label windows, camera keys

  src/parts.js      keycap, switch, outline extrusion, spacer, screw geometry

  src/overlay.js    labels, dimensions, subtitles, end card, readcheck texts, subtitle width check

  tools/            extract_pcb.py, kicad_geom.py, sexp.py, step2mesh.mjs, fetch_cad.sh (data); fetch_fonts.py;

```

- `sh demo/build.sh` takes about 3 minutes on Apple silicon (picture about 60 s with 4 workers). In a clean clone it first rebuilds what git does not carry: `data/case.bin` and `data/pcb.json` from the CAD at the pinned commit (network, and npm for a temporary occt-import-js), the fonts from Google Fonts, and any missing library pack (HDRI, Kokoro, the vcsl / freepats / vsco2ce samples). `FETCH=1` forces the CAD and fonts.
- Checks it runs: `asr_check.py` with `small.en` (two lines carry the words Whisper writes: "RP 2040", "19.05 millimeters"), subtitle single-line widths with the real fonts (widest 552 px against 1500), `readcheck.mjs` (all 19 texts pass), `motioncheck.py` (no one-frame black tiles; motion per second).
- Demo-specific pitfalls: the v4 board file is a panel with breakaway tabs, so the board outline is the 3x6 plate outline inset 0.4 mm (the plate's 21 cutouts sit 0.4 mm off the switch footprints, measured, and corrected); the case STEP has y up and must be flipped and shifted onto the board (offsets in `tools/step2mesh.mjs`), checked by the four screw holes; the project logo footprint is skipped at extraction; the Kokoro voice reads "RP2040" badly, so the spoken text says "R P twenty forty".

# Exploded Teardown — Style Prompt

> A real product, built from its own engineering files (CAD, PCB layout, bill of materials), lit like a studio packshot and taken apart in front of the camera: the layers lift on one axis, the camera travels between them, every part is named with the numbers its files contain, and it closes again into one object.
> References (grammar only): hardware-launch exploded films (layer stagger, orbit timing), repair-guide teardowns (opening order, the macro on the part that matters), engineering drawing (leaders, dimension lines). Never copy their products, layouts, typefaces or music, or name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

A frame reads as this style when:

- **the object is real and exact**: geometry, positions and counts come from the product's own files (STEP, KiCad, BOM, assembly guide). Nothing is eyeballed that a file can give;
- **it is shown apart**: layers float on one axis with even, readable gaps, each still oriented as it sits in the product;
- **it is photographed, not drawn**: physically based materials, a studio key light, a cool rim, an HDRI reflection, soft contact shadow on an invisible floor;
- **the numbers live on the object**: thin leader lines from a dot on the part, dimension lines with ticks drawn in the scene's own perspective, never a table beside it;
- **the camera never stops travelling**: one or a few continuous moves, orbit outside, macro inside.

It is not a glass product render (one object, material beauty, no disassembly), not a blueprint (line drawing on a grid, no light), not a keynote (slides, headline type, a stage), not an assembly manual (step numbers, arrows, hands).

## 2. Materials & rendering

- Real-time PBR (three.js `MeshPhysicalMaterial`) at 2× and downsampled, ambient occlusion, a depth of field with one aperture for wide and macro (blur follows 1/focus − 1/z, so it grows as the camera comes close), a high-threshold bloom for emitters only, a vignette.
- Each material keeps its character: plastics with soft sheen (roughness 0.55–0.7), boards with a thin clearcoat and traces as a raised, lighter relief under the mask, metallic pads, tight highlights on machined metal, matte rubber.
- **Boards are painted from their layout files**: copper pours, every trace, via, pad and drill, silkscreen, on both sides, at 14–20 px per millimetre, with roughness, metalness and bump maps from the same drawing. Components stand at their footprint positions with their package sizes.
- Light: a warm key from above front, a cool rectangular rim behind that follows the camera so edges separate from the ground, a soft top light, a low HDRI for reflections; a practical fill only where the camera goes inside.
- Background: a dark graphite seamless sweep (screen-space radial gradient), floor visible only as soft shadow.
- Effects anchored to the world (leaders, dimension lines, glows) are projected from 3D points every frame; only subtitles and title cards live in screen space.

**Where the geometry comes from.** For the user's own product, ask for its STEP / IGES / KiCad / other CAD exports, BOM and spec sheet before anything else. For a public product, look for open hardware (GitHub, GitLab, OSHWA certification list, Hackaday.io, Printables/Thingiverse sources with the original CAD) and component datasheets from the maker. CC0, public domain, CC BY and MIT are fine with credit; CERN-OHL (-P, -W, -S), CC BY-SA, GPL hardware and "no known restrictions" are not the same thing: name the terms to the user and ask before using them. Without files, build only from published dimensions (datasheet, spec page), say on screen or in the voice that it is a model, and show no number you could not source. Never stand in a generated image for the real part.

Keep a FACTS.md in the project folder (claim, source URL, quoted wording, or the measurement method for anything measured from the CAD) and deliver it with the film.

## 3. Colour logic

- The product brings its own colours; the frame around it is neutral and dark, so the product is always the brightest, most saturated thing.
- Interface ink is one warm white at two strengths (names at full, specs at about 60 %), plus **one accent** reserved for measured things: dimension lines, label indices and one matching detail on the product itself.
- Values are ordered: ground darkest, product mid to light, labels lightest. Never put text on a busy, bright part without a dark backing.
- Example (our demo): ground #34363a → #0d0e10, ink #f1efe9, accent #ff6b3d.

## 4. Type & subtitles

- Names: a clean sans at medium weight in the film's script (28–32 px; Noto Sans SC 500 in our demo). Specs and numbers: a monospaced face (15–22 px; JetBrains Mono) so digits line up and read as measurement. A neutral grotesque (Inter) for Latin running text.
- Label structure is fixed: a two-digit index in the accent, the name, one spec line. Units always written (mm, MB, ×n for counts). A label carries at most one fact the voice does not say.
- Dimension text sits on a small dark plate, follows the line's angle and is never upside down.
- Subtitles: a centred strip at the bottom with a soft shadow and no box; if the film is bilingual, the film's language on top. Hold every cue ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s); every label stays fully in frame for CJK ÷ 4.5 + other ÷ 15 + 1.5 s.

## 5. Motion quality

- 24 fps on ones; everything is smooth and deterministic.
- **Separation**: smooth start, fast middle, long settle (ease-in-out cubed); layers leave top first, 0.15–0.2 s apart; repeated parts (keys, screws) fan out in a wave ordered by distance from a corner.
- **Closing**: bottom first, quicker (about 1 s per layer), the last layer lands with a real mechanical response (a key travels its stroke and returns; nothing bounces like rubber unless it is rubber).
- While held apart, layers may float a millimetre or two with offset phases; during macro shots they hold perfectly still.
- Labels draw in (anchor dot, leader growing, text sliding 10 px) and fade out before the parts move again.
- Never moves: the floor, the light rig's relation to the camera, the label column's x position.

## 6. Camera grammar

| Move | What it expresses | Can serve |
|---|---|---|
| Orbit while layers separate | the whole, its order of assembly | a reveal; a structure overview |
| Grazing macro dolly | touch, material, finish | an opening; a texture |
| Dive between layers | being inside | a hidden component; how it works |
| Slow push on one still part | the part that matters | a chip, a sensor, a seal |
| Rise through the stack | one subsystem to the next | a transition between stops |
| Fast pull back | return, synthesis | a closing; a before/after |
| High three-quarter drift | scale and precision | sizes, pitch, thickness |

- At key moments the subject fills at least a third of the frame height. Labels live in a column on the free side (shift the projection with a view offset rather than moving the object), subtitles in the bottom 12 %.
- Transitions are camera moves through the object itself. No cuts to black, no slide transitions, no split screens.
- The camera path is keyed in the product's own coordinates and interpolated without overshoot (monotone cubic), so a held macro really holds.

## 7. Sound palette

- Instruments: tuned mallets (marimba, vibraphone, glockenspiel, glass), a round bass, a short synthetic kick and small dry percussion. Precise and dry outside the object; sustained and airy inside it.
- Foley is the material: hollow plastic clacks for keycaps or housings, a switch click with a low thock, dry taps for boards, inharmonic rings for small machined metal, a soft thud for the enclosure, airy swooshes for layers lifting and for camera dives, a fine pen hiss when a dimension line draws, a tiny tick per label.
- Every separation and every landing has its sound, panned to where the part is.
- Silence: at least two near-silences (room tone only) before the big separations or the turn back; the first sound after each is the most important hit around it.
- Mix: voice clearly on top (music about 10 dB under it while it speaks), music bus ducked, sub-bass kept lean (20–60 Hz well under the full band), loudness −14 LUFS.
- Voice: calm, close, unhurried, short sentences; numbers spoken as words, written as digits.

## 8. Native moves

- **The wave lift.** Repeated parts rise in a wave across the object. *Fits content like:* battery cells; solar tiles; the drawers of a modular shelf.
- **Inside the gap.** The camera enters the space between two lifted layers to see a hidden face. *Fits content like:* the back of a logic board; the inside of a drone arm; the underside of a sensor module.
- **The leader that lands on the part.** A macro label whose line ends on the component. *Fits content like:* a pressure sensor in a shoe; a gasket in a waterproof case; a motor driver.
- **Dimensions drawn on the thing.** After closing, the real outline gets dimension lines in perspective. *Fits content like:* the thickness of a laptop lid; the footprint of a router; the bore of a valve.
- **One real motion.** A part performs its true mechanical motion once (a press, a hinge, a latch). *Fits content like:* a camera shutter; a buckle; a folding hinge.
- **Lights on inside.** Emitters inside the product switch on while it is apart. *Fits content like:* status LEDs; a backlit display; an indicator ring.

## 9. Pitfalls of the medium

- **Invented numbers.** A size that no file gives. Fix: measure it from the CAD and say "measured" in the facts file, or leave it out.
- **Mixed-up revisions.** Plates, cases and boards from different versions of a project. Fix: check hole positions and stack heights across the files (they must coincide), and pin the commit.
- **Panelised boards.** Layout files may hold a panel with breakaway tabs. Fix: take the outline from a plate or case of the same revision, or flood-fill from an interior point.
- **Zero-length edges.** Duplicate outline points give zero normals → NaN → black squares after bloom. Fix: clean outlines, repair zero normals, scan frames for one-frame black tiles.
- **Overshooting camera splines.** Catmull-Rom over unevenly spaced keys flies past a macro stop. Fix: monotone interpolation per component.
- **Labels too short.** Macro stops last about three seconds. Fix: one fact per label, opened before the camera settles; check with `readcheck`.
- **Over-bright light sweeps.** Area lights blow plastics to white. Fix: sweeps at a fraction of the key, bloom threshold above the brightest diffuse surface.
- **Brand marks on parts.** Chip tops and connector shells carry trademarks. Fix: plain package tops; drop logo footprints unless the product is the user's own.
- **Crushed blacks.** Black plastics against a black ground disappear. Fix: lift them to a dark grey and let the rim light separate them.

## 10. Engine

All in `demo/src/` (three.js r170, the library's `core/three/post.js` and `core/lib.js`):

- `parts.js`: `keycapGeometry(w, d, h)` (lofted shell with a spherical dish and a stem), `switchGeometries()`, `loft(rings)`, `shapeFrom(outline, holes, circles)` (KiCad outline to extrusion), `inset`, `hexSpacer`, `screwGeometry`.
- `pcbtex.js`: `paintPCB(data, side, outline, box, ppm)` paints colour, roughness/metalness and bump maps from extracted layout data.
- `comps.js`: `buildBackParts(data, group, y, materials)` places package bodies at footprint positions and returns anchors.
- `overlay.js`: anchored labels (`label`), perspective dimension lines (`dimension`), subtitles, title card, readcheck texts, subtitle width check.
- `main.js`: layers, explode and gap functions, the camera keys (orbit or eye/target, monotone), lights, `window.EV` for the mixer.
- `tools/extract_pcb.py`, `kicad_geom.py`, `sexp.py`: read any `.kicad_pcb` (outlines, tracks, zones, pads, silkscreen, footprints; plain Python). `tools/step2mesh.mjs`: STEP to mesh.

**Extra packages and packs**, beyond `setup.sh deps [voice] [music]`: `occt-import-js` (npm, LGPL-2.1, not in the library's package.json) to triangulate STEP files, and the studio HDRI (`sh tools/fetch.sh hdri`). Install the npm package yourself into a private `node_modules` in the project folder (as `tools/fetch_cad.sh` does in a temp folder), never into `$LIB`.

Minimal example, not in the demo: read a plate file with `extract_pcb.py`, extrude `shapeFrom(outline, cutouts)` 1.5 mm as aluminium (`metalness: 1, roughness: .35`) and orbit it with three `CAM` keys.

## 11. Variation space

Decided per film: which product and revision, which layers to separate and in what order, how many stops inside and which parts deserve them, the camera route, whether to open from the whole or from a detail, the product's palette and the accent, the voice.

- **Three structures**: one orbit with two stops; a "how it works" path following a signal or flow through the layers; two revisions taken apart side by side, each held still before a difference is named.
- **Three openings**: a part performing its real motion in macro; the closed product turning in silence on the seamless; a single component floating alone before the rest of the product assembles around it.
- **Three endings**: closed with its dimensions drawn on it; closing into a top view that becomes a technical drawing; apart one last time, frozen, every part labelled like a printable sheet.

---

How our demo was made (story, shots, score, title card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

# Sports Telestrator — our demo

One example among many. Don't reuse its story, arc, shots, props or timings.

Demo: *Freeze Frame* (定格, 54.4 s) · `telestrator.mp4` · source in [`demo/`](demo/)

Istanbul, 25 February 2019: Beşiktaş lead Fenerbahçe 3–0 at half-time; Fenerbahçe score three in twelve minutes and draw 3–3. A fictional analysis show, *定格 FREEZE FRAME*, takes the comeback apart goal by goal, each goal with its own technique and the score bar flipping 3–0 → 3–1 → 3–2 → 3–3: the 55th-minute goal frozen mid-play on the pass from the right; the 61st-minute header frozen in two camera angles side by side, then stamped by the VAR check; the 67th-minute equaliser — the decisive one — watched live, rewound and frozen three times (the half-cleared ball, nobody stepping out, a strike 0.84 s after receiving, from outside the box), then seen from the reverse replay. Finally the strike frame flattens into a top-down board where all three shooting positions land: two from close range, one from 27 metres. A data card repeats the counted numbers; the hero's minute and name close it.

This is an unofficial fan analysis made from real broadcast footage released under CC BY by the broadcaster itself (beIN SPORTS Türkiye, on its verified YouTube channel; one clip via Wikimedia Commons), a CC BY photo and a CC0 photo. The show is fictional; beIN SPORTS, the clubs and the league did not make or endorse it. Every fact is quoted in [`demo/FACTS.md`](demo/FACTS.md); the licence check is in [`demo/SOURCES.md`](demo/SOURCES.md).

The CC BY rests on the broadcaster's own licence statement on YouTube (checked 2026-10-21; evidence in `demo/tools/license-evidence.json`); we cannot see the rights chain from league and clubs to broadcaster. Hosting the film here with full attribution is what the licence allows, but re-uploads to video platforms may still be matched by Content ID. A film made in this style for your own topic should use your own footage, or footage whose licence you have checked the same way.

## Story & structure

Shape: a chronological build to the deep breakdown, then a summary. Sting and match-record card (0–5.2 s) set up 0–3 and bracket the three second-half goals. Goal one (5.2–10.6) and goal two (10.6–17.8) are light treatments, so the third keeps the full grammar to itself (17.8–36.8). The shot map (36.8–42.6) is the only new idea after the breakdown: where the three were struck. The data card (42.6–47.0), the 67′ slate (47.0–49.6) and the end card (49.6–54.4) close.

Formats spent, each once and each for a new fact: show sting; match-record card with a goal timeline and a marker bracket; live play with commentary transcript; freeze-in-play; dual-angle split-screen freeze; VAR stamp; score-bar flips (three); tape rewind; three spotlight freezes with rings, a red space patch, cyan link lines, the traced box line; slow motion with a running-trail ring; frame-counting stopwatch; ball comet; reverse replay with its own freeze; perspective flatten into a shot map; data card with a polaroid; hero slate; end card.

## Score structure

- 120 BPM, E minor, sampled band: MuldjordKit drums, electric bass, staccato trumpet and trombone, timpani, horn, cellos, glockenspiel.
- The groove restarts at the head of each played segment (full in the record card and the data card, low under live play so the commentary leads, half-time in slow play and the split screen). Every freeze is a brass stab + timpani + thump + shutter, then hi-hat only: the drums stop with the picture.
- Goals: big brass chord with crash and glockenspiel on each score-bar flip; the VAR stamp lands on low timpani, trombone and crash.
- Shot map: stab on the cut, a timpani roll building under the flatten, a second stab when the board settles, glockenspiel B–D–E as the three rows land, then half-time groove.
- Slate and end card: big chord, horns and cellos held in E minor, two glockenspiel strokes, fade with the picture.
- Natural sound: the broadcaster's commentary and crowd at full level in live play, a low-passed crowd bed under freezes, the goal roars aligned to the goal frames.
- Voice: Kokoro `bm_george`, 8 lines at speed 1.1; names spelled for the voice ("Zayits", "Saduk"), real spelling in the subtitles.

Demo-specific choices and pitfalls: the first two goals come from the broadcaster's full summary, which turned out to be the source of the Commons clip (its file page cites the video), so all footage is one CC BY release; the Commons page has no licence-review stamp, so the licence was checked on the video page itself (verified channel, CC BY field), see `demo/SOURCES.md`. Sources disagree on the first goal's assist (Valbuena vs Dirar), so the film names neither and shows "No. 17 from the right"; the official goal list (55′ / 61′ / 67′) wins over match reports that say 62′ and 66′. A "far corner" claim in one report contradicts the footage, so the third goal's corner is not mentioned. The split-screen windows first slid in unclipped and showed the broadcaster's URL for a few frames; each window is now clipped to its slice in source coordinates. The VAR stamp first landed before the ball crossed the line; the segment was lengthened so it lands after F057. Record card, shot map, data card and end card were lengthened (not slowed) until every row they carry passes the reading check.

# Sports Telestrator — Style Prompt

> The TV football analysis segment: play the clip at full speed, rewind, freeze it, and draw on the broadcast picture — rings under players' feet, marker arrows for the ball, a red patch for the space nobody covered — then play on, switch angles, count the frames, and flatten the pitch into a board. Real match footage is the ground; every line is drawn on top of it and moves with it. A studio show's packaging (sting, corner bug, score bar, a yellow wipe) holds it together. 16:9.
> References (grammar only): touch-screen analysis segments in televised football (the "telestrator" pundit's board), and explainer channels that annotate real match footage. Never copy a broadcaster's or channel's logo, fonts, colours, idents or graphics, and never name them in the film.

## 1. Essence, and what it is not

1. **Watch it, then take it apart.** Every piece of action is seen moving before it is explained. A freeze always follows play; the explanation never comes first.
2. **One freeze, one finding.** Each freeze says one thing (the ball wasn't cleared; nobody stepped out; he struck it from outside the box) with one label and at most two groups of lines. The same few seconds of footage are reused, each pass going one layer deeper.
3. **Drawn on the real picture.** Rings sit under feet, arrows follow the ball's real path, the box line is traced over the real line. Nothing floats in an abstract diagram until the film deliberately flattens the pitch.
4. **Data counted from the footage.** Times come from frame counts (a stopwatch that runs on source frames), distances from the pitch markings (a perspective transform). What the footage can't measure (ball speed, sprint distance) is not stated.
5. **Studio energy.** Bright marker lines, a white flash and a punch on every freeze, the music stopping with the picture.

Not **Visual Investigation** (that is restrained, synchronised multi-camera evidence where the timeline is the protagonist; this is a pundit's show with packaging and enthusiasm). Not a **highlight reel** (no montage of goals to music; each clip is analysed). Not **Data Storytelling** or an infographic: charts are not the film; the top-down board appears once, as a summary, and is reached by flattening the real picture.

## 2. Frame and layout (1920×1080)

- **Full-frame footage** most of the time. The packaging lives in the corners:
  - **Corner bug**, top right (x 1452–1880, y 38–110): show name on a yellow block + a mode line in the mode's colour — LIVE (red dot) / ANALYSIS (yellow) / REPLAY (cyan). It is in every footage frame from frame 1, because it sits over the broadcaster's logo.
  - **Score bar**, bottom right (x 1392–1880, y 926–996): HOME n – n AWAY + minute. The away number flips on the frame the ball crosses the line (a 0.5 s roll with a yellow flash). It sits over the broadcaster's URL.
  - **Source clock**, top left (x 40–370, y 38–90), on every analysis shot: `❚❚ 04.20s F106` — source seconds and frame number; ▶ ½ in slow motion, ◀◀ in a rewind. Hidden in live play.
- **Labels** (black card, coloured left bar, Chinese line + small spaced English line) sit in empty grass or crowd, never over the action they describe.
- **Subtitle bar** bottom, centred at x 880 (its right edge stays left of the score bar), y 938–1044.
- **Split screen**: two 960×1080 vertical windows, each a 960-px-wide slice of a 1920 frame at 1:1 (no extra scaling), a 6 px yellow divider between them, a camera label at each window's top left (A MAIN CAMERA / B HIGH REVERSE). The slices are chosen so the broadcaster's logo and URL fall outside them.
- **Board pages** (shot map, data card): dark board `#0C1411` with a faint 60 px grid; left column text, right side drawing. No headers, no centred title-and-bullets.

## 3. Editing grammar

- **Order inside one piece of action:** live at 1× (original sound) → rewind (0.6 s, reversed with tracking bars and ◀◀) → freeze ① → slow play (0.6–0.85×, frame-blended) → freeze ② → slow play with a stopwatch → freeze ③ → ball flight with a comet trail → another angle (replay), possibly one more freeze.
- **Lighter variants** for secondary pieces of action, so the deep breakdown stays special:
  - **Freeze-in-play**: no rewind; play at 1× up to the decisive pass, freeze, draw, then play on to the goal.
  - **Dual-angle freeze**: both angles play side by side and each arrives at the same instant (each at its own speed) where both freeze together; the same player is ringed in both.
- **Freeze length** 1.8–2.4 s; a freeze longer than ~2.5 s needs a second action inside it. Two to four freezes per piece of action; more than four, split with a replay.
- **Cuts between segments**: only the packaging wipe — a yellow slanted band with dark edges crossing the frame in 0.34 s. Inside a segment, hard cuts. No dissolves, no page turns.
- **Comparison frames** (the shot map, the data card) are fully drawn early and held ≥ 2.5 s before the next cut.

## 4. Colour identity (the one rule that matters)

| Role | Colour |
|---|---|
| The team/player we follow, the ball, main marker lines | `#FFD400` fluorescent yellow |
| Opponents (rings, block arrows, link lines) | `#3FD8FF` cyan |
| Space (a patch nobody covers) | `#FF3B30` red, fill 0.34–0.38 + dashed edge |
| Pitch lines traced, neutral marks, stamps | `#F4F1E8` chalk |
| Show board | `#0C1411` ink green-black |
| Label / bug background | `rgba(8,12,14,0.9)`; opaque `#080C0E` where it covers a logo |

One colour, one identity, throughout the film: a label's left bar takes the colour of what it names. Change the hues if the show needs to, never the three roles.

## 5. Type

- Labels: Noto Sans SC 900, 40 px (30 px for a name), English line Barlow Condensed 600, 21 px, letter-spacing 2 px, in the role colour.
- Packaging numbers (score, minute, stopwatch, big data): Barlow Condensed 800 Italic.
- Clock / frame numbers: IBM Plex Mono 500, 24 px.
- Board pages: title Noto Sans SC 900 60–64 px, rows Noto Sans SC 700 34–42 px with a grey note under each, numbers Barlow Condensed 800 Italic 64–150 px in yellow; text appears left to right with a clip reveal.
- **No handwriting fonts** anywhere: printed type on a dark card belongs to the same packaging; handwriting reads as a school notebook.
- Subtitles: Chinese line (Noto Sans SC 500, 38 px) above an English line (Barlow Condensed 600, 32 px), black bar 0.64 with a 4 px yellow edge; one line per language, never wrapped — shorten the line instead of shrinking it.
- All fonts OFL from Google Fonts, subset to the characters used (`demo/tools/fonts.py`).

## 6. Motion and drawing

- **Freeze entry**: white flash 0.1 s (0.55) + punch 1.035 → 1.0 in 0.35 s (ease-out) + desaturate 42 % + a cool cast + heavier vignette; then a slow 1.2 % creep. Overlays use the same transform as the picture, or they slide off the players.
- **Spotlight**: everything outside a focus ellipse darkens to 0.42 (even-odd hole), 0.3 s fade.
- **Marker line**: dark outline (w + 6, black 0.55) + coloured core with glow 18 + thin white highlight (w × 0.28); drawn along its length; an arrowhead pops in over the last 10 %; deterministic small wobble at the vertices so it feels hand-drawn. Dashed for intended or future paths (a cross, a run), solid for what happened.
- **Ring**: perspective ellipse (ry = 0.36 r) under the feet, drawn clockwise, outer dashed ring rotating at 60 px/s; a vertical light beam while the player moves.
- **Draw order inside a freeze**: ring (who) → area or link (what happened) → label (the one-line finding), 0.3–0.6 s apart.
- **Slow motion**: source frames at 0.6–0.85×, neighbours cross-blended (no stutter).
- **Rewind**: the clip reversed in 0.6 s (ease-in-out), ±13 px horizontal jitter, four white tracking bars, a big ◀◀ and the word REWIND.
- **Trails**: in screen space keep only the last ~0.6 s (ball 0.24 s) — the camera pans, so long trails land in the wrong place.
- **Stamp** (e.g. a VAR decision): a framed card that drops from 1.7× to 1× with overshoot, slightly rotated, with a small flash — once per film.
- **Perspective flatten**: see Native moves 7.

## 7. Grade and image quality

- Footage: `hqdn3d=1.2:1.2:2.5:2.5` → lanczos to 1920×1080 (modern footage at most 1.5×) → `unsharp=5:5:0.55` → `eq=saturation=0.9:contrast=1.04:gamma=0.97` + slightly cool shadows; one grade for every clip; film grain 2 added once at the master (`mux.sh`).
- Broadcaster logos and URLs are covered by the packaging (bug and score bar placed exactly over them, present from frame 1), or kept outside split-screen windows — never by cropping past 1.5×.
- Prefer a broadcaster's native resolution over an "AI-upscaled" stream.

## 8. Sound palette

- **Layers**: English voice-over (one line per freeze, ≈2.5–3 s) → match sound (commentary + crowd at full level in live play; under freezes only a low-passed crowd bed, looped; the goal roar on the goal frame) → score → foley. Voice ducks everything else to 0.55.
- **Score**: sampled band (drum kit, electric bass, staccato trumpet and trombone, timpani, horn, cellos, glockenspiel), about 120 BPM. The groove restarts at the head of each played segment, so cuts don't need a global bar grid. **On a freeze the drums stop**: one brass stab + timpani + low thump + camera shutter, then only closed hi-hat — the music freezes with the picture. Goals: a big brass chord with crash and glockenspiel on the score-bar flip.
- **Foley**: marker squeak (2–5 kHz band-passed noise with flutter) for each line, pops for rings, a tick per landed label, whoosh on every wipe, tape-motor whine on a rewind, a stopwatch tick every 0.2 s, a thump for the stamp, a long whoosh and a timpani roll under the flatten.
- Mix limited before `mux.sh` normalises to −14 LUFS.

## 9. Native moves (and how the code does them)

1. **Freeze and draw** — a freeze segment = one source frame + flash + punch + desaturate + spotlight; overlays drawn by progress (`overlayAnalysis()`, `overlayG1()` in `demo/index.html`).
2. **Tracked ring** — hand keyframes of the feet point in source pixels every ~3–6 frames, linearly interpolated (`TRK`, `at()`); check them with `?dbg=1`, which paints every tracked point in magenta.
3. **Frame-counting stopwatch** — starts at the receiving frame and counts source frames ÷ fps; stops and turns yellow on the strike (`stopwatch()`).
4. **Score-bar flip on the goal frame**, one entry per goal (`GOALS`, `scoreAt()`, `bugScore()`).
5. **Packaging over watermarks** — corner bug and score bar positioned from the logo and URL coordinates, drawn from frame 1 (`bugTop()`, `bugScore()`).
6. **Dual-angle freeze** — two windows, each its own clip and frame range, both reaching their freeze frame on the same beat; overlays drawn in each window's source coordinates (`splitView()`, `overlayG2()`).
7. **Perspective flatten into a shot map** — for each shot, mark 6–8 known pitch points in its own frame (box and six-yard corners, where the penalty arc meets the box line; FIFA dimensions) and fit a ground-plane homography by least squares (`demo/tools/homography.py` reads `tools/pitch.json`, writes `assets/pitch.json`; residuals ≤ 6 px are fine). The strike frame is then drawn as a mesh of triangles in pitch coordinates (1.5 m cells), each vertex moving from its image position to its board position, each triangle affine-mapped (`drawTri()`); the picture fades out as the chalk board takes over, and the other shots' feet points, converted with their own frames' matrices, drop onto the same board (`shotMap()`). The broadcaster's URL is painted out of the source frame first, because the flatten drags it into the middle of the screen.
8. **Data card** — the counted numbers re-stated on a board page: label left, big yellow number right, red marker circle on the key one (`notes()`).
9. **Commentary transcript** — original-language words with timecodes and a translation, in a small box during live play; inaudible words become an ellipsis, never a guess (`transcript()`).

## 10. Material

1. **Ask the user first** whether they have their own footage (club or academy video, their own camera, a licensed broadcast clip), line-ups, event data or photos, and the rights to use them. Their material comes first.
2. **Where to look** (judge every file on its own page):
   - **Wikimedia Commons** (search "goal", the match, the player): many clips are cut from broadcasters' own YouTube uploads under CC BY. Fine: CC0, public domain, CC BY. Not used: CC BY-SA, "no known restrictions", unclear licences.
   - **A broadcaster's or club's own YouTube channel** when its video page says *Creative Commons Attribution license (reuse allowed)*: check that the channel is the rights holder's official, verified channel (not a re-upload or a fan mirror), save the evidence (channel id, verification, licence field, date checked), and download the native resolution, not an AI-upscaled stream. Third-party re-uploads, fan mirrors, colourised or "restored" versions are never used.
   - **Facts** (scores, minutes, how a goal was scored): the league's or broadcaster's own match page or video description, then established newspapers; quote them in `FACTS.md`. When sources disagree, use the official list and leave the disputed detail out.
   - Photos of players: Commons (CC BY / CC0); state the year when the photo isn't from the match.
3. **Before downloading, tell the user** what you will fetch, from where and under which licence. The finder copied into this style, `demo/tools/footage.py` (`search commons|archive|nasa`, `fetch`, `used`, `md`), logs licence, author, page and the seconds used into `SOURCES.jsonl` and writes `SOURCES.md`; `demo/tools/fetch_sources.sh` shows how a verified YouTube CC BY source is fetched with `uvx yt-dlp`. Wikimedia rate-limits bursts (HTTP 429): one request at a time.
4. **People on screen**: players, referees and staff in the event are fine; never slow down or freeze on an identifiable spectator.

## 11. Engine

Canvas 2D, one page: `window.render(t)` is async and deterministic, frames load on demand from JPEG sequences (one folder per clip, 90-frame cache). `timeline.json` (segments with clip and source frame range, voice lines) drives the page, `tools/mix.py` and `tools/cues.py`. `window.TEXTS(t)` reports the text that must be read, for `readcheck.mjs`. `core/render/video.mjs` renders at 30 fps.

## 12. Pitfalls

- **Wrong tracking points** are the biggest risk: reading coordinates off a scaled contact sheet is easily 20–50 px off. Read them on full-resolution crops with a pixel ruler, then check with `?dbg=1`.
- **Overlays not under the punch transform** slide off the players during a freeze.
- **Balls vanish**: long shots are a few pixels with motion blur; colour tracking loses them; frames where the ball is invisible are interpolated and the number says "≈".
- **Numbers the footage can't support** (ball speed, distance run) are not written. Distances only from a homography fitted to visible markings, each shot in its own frame (the camera zooms and pans between shots).
- **Packaging late by one frame** shows the logo: bugs never fade in over footage.
- **Split-screen windows sliding in** reveal what's outside them (a logo, a URL): clip each window to its slice in source coordinates, not only to the screen half.
- **Score state must match the moment**: before the 67th-minute goal it is 3–2, not 3–3.
- **Names in TTS**: spell them phonetically for the voice ("Zayits", "Saduk") and keep the real spelling in subtitles; record the ASR result for proper names in `lines.json` (`asr`).
- **Freeze labels echo the subtitle** and live only ~1 s; anything the viewer must read (scores, board rows, the data card) gets ≥ 2.5 s and goes into `TEXTS`.

## 13. Variation space

The agent decides per film: the sport (football, basketball pick-and-roll with screens drawn as bars, tennis rallies with landing zones, F1 overtakes with racing lines — anything with a wide camera that shows the whole play), the moments, the show's fictional name and colours (keeping the three roles), how many freezes.

- **Three structures:** chronological build-up to the deep breakdown (secondary moments get light treatments, the decisive one the full rewind-and-freeze); one moment taken apart from three angles; a "what went wrong" defensive breakdown ending on the space map.
- **Three openings:** the show sting into a match-record card; the goal frame frozen in the first second, then rewind; the stopwatch running over live play.
- **Three endings:** the top-down board that sums up the moments; the data card with one number circled; the hero shot slowed with the minute and name.
